reasoning/analogy.sol: ACE: A(1)→C(3) +2, C(3)→E(5) +2. HKN: H(8)→K(11) +3, K(11)→N(14) +3. Pattern in first set is +2, second set is +3. Working backwards from QTW: Q(17)→T(20) +3, T(20)→W(23) +3. So we need +2 pattern: ? → Q. Reverse of Q(17) - 3 = 14 = N, minus 3 = 11 = K. So NKN? Not an option. Actually, ACE to HKN: A→H = +7, C→K = +8, E→N = +9. So each letter advances by increasing amounts. From HKN to MPS: H→M = +5, K→P = +5, N→S = +5. That gives +5 each. So MPS: M(13)+5=Q, P(16)+5=T, S(19)+5=W. MPS works!

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: 1. All birds are animals. 2. No animal is a fish. Conclusions: I. No bird is a fish. II. Some animals are birds.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: All birds are inside animals. No animal is fish, so birds cannot be fish either → I follows. Since all birds are animals, there is definitely at least some overlap → some animals are birds (the same set of birds) → II follows. Both conclusions follow.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: 1. Some books are pens. 2. All pens are tables. Conclusions: I. Some books are tables. II. Some tables are pens.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Some books are pens, and all pens are tables → those books which are pens are also tables → Some books are tables (I follows). All pens are tables → there exists at least one pen that is a table → Some tables are pens (II follows). Both follow.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: 1. No apple is a mango. 2. All mangoes are fruits. Conclusions: I. No apple is a fruit. II. Some fruits are mangoes.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: No direct relation between apple and fruit is given. Apples could be fruits or not → I does not follow. All mangoes are fruits → there exist mangoes that are fruits → some fruits are mangoes (II follows). Only II follows.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: 1. Some cups are plates. 2. No plate is a bowl. Conclusions: I. Some cups are not bowls. II. No cup is a bowl.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Some cups are plates. No plate is a bowl. So those cups which are plates cannot be bowls → some cups are definitely not bowls → I follows. However, there could be other cups (not plates) that are bowls, so we cannot say 'no cup is a bowl' → II does not follow. Only I follows.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: 1. All dogs are cats. 2. All cats are animals. Conclusions: I. All dogs are animals. II. Some animals are dogs.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: All dogs are cats, all cats are animals → by transitive property, all dogs are animals → I follows. Since all dogs are animals, there exists at least one dog that is an animal → some animals are dogs → II follows. Both follow.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All pens are pencils. No pencil is an eraser. Conclusions: I. No pen is an eraser. II. Some pencils are pens.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: All pens inside pencils. No pencil is eraser, so pens cannot be erasers (I). All pens are pencils means some pencils are pens (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: Some apples are bananas. All bananas are cherries. Conclusions: I. Some apples are cherries. II. All cherries are bananas.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Apples that are bananas are also cherries (I). But all cherries need not be bananas - there could be cherries that are not bananas.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: No cat is dog. All dogs are animals. Conclusions: I. No cat is animal. II. Some animals are dogs.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Cats and dogs no overlap. Dogs inside animals, but cats and animals may overlap. Cannot conclude I. All dogs are animals means some animals are dogs (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All flowers are plants. Some plants are trees. Conclusions: I. Some flowers are trees. II. All trees are plants.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Flowers inside plants. Some plants are trees - those trees may differ from flowers. Cannot say flowers and trees overlap.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: Some pens are pencils. Some pencils are sharpeners. Conclusions: I. Some pens are sharpeners. II. All sharpeners are pencils.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Some pens are pencils and some pencils are sharpeners. But the pens that are pencils may not be the same pencils that are sharpeners. No definite relation.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All books are pages. No page is a cover. Conclusions: I. No book is a cover. II. Some pages are books.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Books inside pages. Pages no overlap with covers, so books no overlap with covers (I). All books are pages means some pages are books (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: Some doctors are engineers. All engineers are scientists. Conclusions: I. Some doctors are scientists. II. All scientists are engineers.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Doctors that are engineers are also scientists since all engineers are scientists (I). But all scientists need not be engineers.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: No mango is orange. Some oranges are sweet. Conclusions: I. No mango is sweet. II. Some oranges are not sweet.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Mangoes and oranges no overlap. Oranges that are sweet have no relation to mangoes. "Some oranges are sweet" does not mean some are not sweet.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All birds are animals. All animals are living beings. Conclusions: I. All birds are living beings. II. Some living beings are birds.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Birds inside animals inside living beings (I). All birds are living beings means some living beings are birds (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: Some professors are researchers. No researcher is a student. Conclusions: I. Some professors are not students. II. Some students are professors.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Some professors are researchers. Since no researcher is a student, those professors who are researchers are not students (I).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All tigers are mammals. No mammal is a reptile. Conclusions: I. No tiger is a reptile. II. Some mammals are tigers.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Tigers are mammals. No mammal is reptile, so tigers cannot be reptiles (I). All tigers are mammals means some mammals are tigers (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: Some vegetables are fruits. No fruit is a grain. Conclusions: I. Some vegetables are not grains. II. Some fruits are not grains.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Some vegetables are fruits. No fruit is grain, so those vegetables which are fruits are not grains (I). "No fruit is grain" means all fruits are not grains (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All balls are round. Some round objects are red. Conclusions: I. Some balls are red. II. Some red objects are round.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All students are hardworking. Some hardworking people are successful. Conclusions: I. Some students are successful. II. Some successful people are hardworking.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Students are inside hardworking people. Some hardworking are successful - may not be students. "Some hardworking are successful" = "some successful are hardworking" (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All pens are pencils. No pencil is an eraser. Conclusions: I. No pen is an eraser. II. Some pencils are pens.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: All pens inside pencils. No pencil is eraser, so pens cannot be erasers (I). All pens are pencils means some pencils are pens (II).

reasoning/syllogism.sol: Apples that are bananas are also cherries (I). But all cherries need not be bananas - there could be cherries that are not bananas.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: No cat is dog. All dogs are animals. Conclusions: I. No cat is animal. II. Some animals are dogs.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Cats and dogs no overlap. Dogs inside animals, but cats and animals may overlap. Cannot conclude I. All dogs are animals means some animals are dogs (II).

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: All flowers are plants. Some plants are trees. Conclusions: I. Some flowers are trees. II. All trees are plants.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Flowers inside plants. Some plants are trees - those trees may differ from flowers. Cannot say flowers and trees overlap.

reasoning/syllogism.text: Statements: Some pens are pencils. Some pencils are sharpeners. Conclusions: I. Some pens are sharpeners. II. All sharpeners are pencils.
reasoning/syllogism.sol: Some pens are pencils and some pencils are sharpeners. But the pens that are pencils may not be the same pencils that are sharpeners. No definite relation.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a linear seating arrangement, the concepts of leftmost and rightmost are described as absolute references. What does this imply about the ends of the row?

options.t: The leftmost position changes depending on the perspective of the seated persons.
The leftmost and rightmost positions are fixed and do not change regardless of perspective.
Only the rightmost position is absolute; the leftmost is relative.
Neither end is fixed; both are relative to the observer.

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The lesson states that because the row has two distinct ends, the concepts of leftmost and rightmost are absolute references that never change regardless of the perspective of the individuals seated. This absolute frame of reference makes linear puzzles straightforward. Therefore, the ends are fixed and do not vary with viewpoint.

reasoning/puzzles.text: Which category of clue does the statement "A sits third to the left of B" belong to in a linear arrangement puzzle?
reasoning/puzzles.sol: The lesson classifies clues into definite, relative, and negative. A definite clue pins an entity to a specific slot (e.g., "D sits at the left end"). A relative clue describes the positional relationship between two entities without fixing either absolutely; typical forms include "A is second to the left of B". The given statement matches this definition, so it is a relative clue.

reasoning/puzzles.text: What is the primary function of negative clues in linear seating arrangement puzzles?

options.t: They directly assign a person to a specific seat.
They create a set of possible pairs of slots for two persons.
They eliminate impossible slots and prune the search space.
They link two separate arrangement models together.

reasoning/puzzles.sol: According to the lesson, negative clues state where an entity cannot be (e.g., "H is not at either end"). Although they do not place anyone directly, negative clues are powerful because they prune the search space and often resolve ambiguities left by relative clues. Thus, their main role is elimination of impossible slots.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a circular seating arrangement where all persons face the centre, the direction "clockwise" corresponds to which relative side for each person?
reasoning/puzzles.sol: The lesson explains that facing inside versus facing outside changes the mapping of clockwise/anticlockwise to left/right. When persons face the centre, their right side points in the clockwise direction and their left side points anticlockwise. Hence, clockwise is equivalent to the right side for each individual.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a sequencing puzzle, the clue "Event C occurs immediately after Event D" translates into which constraints in the directed graph representation?

options.t: An edge D → C and a restriction that no other event can be placed between D and C.
No edge is added; it only fixes the rank of C.

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The lesson states that a clue like "C immediately after D" adds edges D → C and also forbids any other event between D and C. This is stricter than simple precedence (which would only add D → C). Therefore, the correct representation includes both the precedence edge and the immediate‑precedence restriction.

reasoning/puzzles.text: A puzzle contains the clues: (1) Either A sits at the left end or B sits at the right end, but not both. (2) If A sits at the left end, then C sits immediately to the right of D. Which solving technique does the lesson recommend for such layered conditionality?

options.t: Treat both conditionals as always active and apply them simultaneously
Create two parallel scenarios assuming each disjunct true and solve each independently
Ignore the exclusive‑or clue and only use the conditional clue
Assume both disjuncts are true at the same time

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The lesson describes an exclusive‑or (XOR) combined with a conditional clue. The correct method is scenario‑splitting: create one branch where A is at the left end (making the conditional active) and another where B is at the right end (making the conditional inactive). Solve each branch independently; if both yield complete arrangements, the answer must be invariant across them. Treating the conditional as always active or ignoring the XOR leads to false eliminations, while assuming both disjuncts true violates the XOR.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a multi‑attribute matrix puzzle, a relational clue states: "The engineer likes cricket." How should this clue be processed during constraint propagation?

options.t: Assign both attributes directly to the engineer without checking other entities
Intersect the candidate sets of the two linked attributes for that entity; if the intersection becomes a singleton, fix the value and cascade eliminations
Eliminate all other values for those attributes across all entities immediately
Treat the clue as a negative clue and remove the engineer‑cricket pair from all entities

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The multi‑attribute matrix method uses cross‑attribute propagation. For a clue linking two attributes of the same entity, the solver intersects the candidate sets of those attributes for that entity. If the intersection reduces to a single value, that value is fixed for the entity, and the elimination cascades to other entities sharing the same attribute value. Direct assignment without intersection, blanket elimination, or treating it as a negative clue would ignore the constraint‑propagation mechanism described.

reasoning/puzzles.text: A hybrid puzzle includes an arithmetic constraint: the sum of the floor numbers of three persons equals 12. Each person occupies a distinct floor from 1 to 5. What must the solver ensure when applying this constraint?

options.t: Treat the sum constraint as independent of the distinctness requirement
Combine the arithmetic constraint with the permutation of distinct values to prune domains
Ignore distinctness because the sum already limits possibilities
Assume floors can repeat to satisfy the sum

reasoning/puzzles.sol: Hybrid puzzles with quantitative constraints require integrating arithmetic restrictions with the permutation of distinct values. The solver must consider the sum together with the fact that floors are distinct and drawn from 1‑5, which prunes the domain of each person’s floor. Ignoring distinctness or treating the sum in isolation would miss deductions and could allow invalid repetitions, while assuming repeats contradicts the puzzle’s distinct‑value rule.

reasoning/puzzles.text: When solving an optimization puzzle that asks for the number of valid arrangements, the lesson advises branching on the most ambiguous variable. Which heuristic guarantees the smallest search tree?

options.t: Choose the variable with the largest domain first
Choose the variable with the smallest remaining domain (MRV)
Branch randomly to explore diverse possibilities
Always place the first person mentioned in the clues

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The lesson explicitly states the MRV (minimum remaining values) heuristic: always place the person or attribute with the fewest possible positions next. This mirrors the "most constrained first" principle from AI and ensures the search tree remains shallow because the branching factor is limited by the most restricted variable. Choosing the largest domain, random branching, or a fixed order does not guarantee minimal search effort.

reasoning/puzzles.text: According to the lesson, adding conditional clues, arithmetic constraints, or optimisation objectives makes the general puzzle problem NP‑complete. However, exam instances are bounded. What practical algorithm is recommended for solving such puzzles under time pressure?

options.t: Depth‑first search with constraint propagation (maintaining arc consistency) and MRV heuristic
Apply Hopcroft‑Karp bipartite matching for every puzzle

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The lesson notes that while the general case is NP‑complete, exam puzzles have ≤12 entities and high clue density, making the constraint graph almost tree‑like. The recommended practical algorithm is a depth‑first search with constraint propagation (maintaining arc consistency) combined with the MRV variable‑ordering heuristic. This solves any exam‑level puzzle within seconds on paper. Exhaustive enumeration is infeasible, topological sorting only handles pure precedence, and Hopcroft‑Karp is specific to bipartite matching in double‑row puzzles.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a circular table with 8 equally spaced seats, A sits opposite B. If A is anchored at seat 1, which seat must B occupy?
reasoning/puzzles.sol: Opposite seats on an even‑sized circle are separated by half the total seats. With 8 seats, half is 4 steps. Starting from seat 1 and moving clockwise 4 positions lands on seat 5 (1→2→3→4→5). The 180° rotational flip would map seat 1 to itself and seat 5 to itself, so the opposite relation uniquely fixes B at seat 5. Therefore the correct seat is 5.

reasoning/puzzles.text: A multi‑attribute puzzle assigns each person a profession and a floor. The clue "The engineer lives on the third floor" is processed by arc consistency (AC‑3). How are the domains pruned?

options.t: Removes all floors except third from engineer's floor domain and removes engineer from other persons' profession domains
Removes only the third floor from engineer's floor domain
Adds engineer to all persons' profession domains

reasoning/puzzles.sol: AC‑3 enforces binary constraints. The clue gives a unary restriction on the engineer's floor domain (only floor 3 remains) and a binary all‑different constraint on professions: since each profession is unique, "engineer" is eliminated from the profession domain of every other person. This simultaneous pruning of the floor and profession domains is exactly what arc consistency achieves for such a direct clue.

reasoning/puzzles.text: A conditional clue states: "If P sits at position 2 then Q sits at position 4." In an implication graph used for conditional clause chains, how is this clue represented?

options.t: As a directed edge from node (P=2) to node (Q=4)
As an undirected edge between P and Q
As a bidirectional edge between (P=2) and (Q=4)

reasoning/puzzles.sol: Implication graphs treat each possible assignment as a node. A conditional "If antecedent then consequent" becomes a directed edge from the antecedent node (P=2) to the consequent node (Q=4). The edge is activated only when the antecedent becomes true during search; it does not create a permanent binary constraint nor a bidirectional link. This representation allows unit propagation to fire Q=4 automatically once P=2 is assigned.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a linear row of 6 seats, A is to the left of B with at least one person sitting between them. What is the minimum possible number of seats separating A and B?
reasoning/puzzles.sol: "At least one person between" means the positional difference must be ≥2 seats (e.g., A at seat 1, one person at seat 2, B at seat 3). The distance measured as the number of seats from A to B exclusive of A but inclusive of B is 2. Any smaller gap would place B immediately next to A, violating the condition. Hence the minimum separation is 2 seats.

reasoning/puzzles.text: Floors are numbered 1 to 4. The clue "The engineer's floor number is the square of the teacher's floor number" appears. Which teacher–engineer floor pair is forced by this arithmetic constraint?
reasoning/puzzles.sol: We need integer floors t (teacher) and e (engineer) with e = t² and both in {1,2,3,4}. Testing t=1 gives e=1 (valid but does not use the square relation uniquely). t=2 gives e=4 (both within range). t=3 gives e=9 (out of range). t=4 gives e=16 (out of range). Only the pair (2,4) satisfies the square relation while keeping both floors inside the allowed domain, so the clue deterministically fixes teacher=2 and engineer=4.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a circular seating puzzle, fixing one person breaks rotational symmetry. What additional clue is needed to eliminate the remaining reflection symmetry?

options.t: A clue stating the person faces north
A clue stating two persons are adjacent
A clue stating the number of persons is even
A clue stating the table has a diameter

reasoning/puzzles.sol: A circular arrangement has dihedral symmetry Dn. Fixing one person removes the rotational part, but a reflection (180° flip) may still map the arrangement onto itself. An asymmetric clue such as "A faces north" distinguishes the two mirror images because facing direction changes under reflection. Adjacency, even count, or table diameter do not break the reflection symmetry. Therefore, a facing clue is required.

reasoning/puzzles.text: Which propagation method is necessary to enforce a global cardinality constraint like "exactly three doctors" in a seating puzzle?

options.t: Flow-based filtering on a bipartite graph

reasoning/puzzles.sol: Global cardinality constraints couple many variables simultaneously. Pairwise arc consistency only checks binary relations and cannot guarantee that the overall count of a value (e.g., doctors) can be satisfied. The standard algorithm builds a flow network: source to variable nodes (capacity 1), variable to value nodes (capacity 1), value nodes to sink with capacity equal to the allowed maximum (and lower bound for minimum). A feasible flow proves GCC consistency, and edges carrying zero flow in all maximum flows are pruned. This flow-based filtering is stronger than AC-3.

reasoning/puzzles.text: When multiple step-size clues are given on a circular arrangement, which invariant must be checked to avoid inconsistency?

options.t: The sum of all step sizes must equal the number of persons
The parity (even/odd) of the distance between any two persons must be consistent across all clues
The step sizes must all be prime numbers
The clockwise distance must always be less than the anticlockwise distance

reasoning/puzzles.sol: Step-size clues on a circle fix distances modulo the number of persons. If several clues relate the same pair of persons through different paths, the parity (mod 2) of the resulting distances must agree; otherwise the clues contradict. For example, if one clue says A is 3 steps clockwise from B (odd distance) and another implies an even distance between them, the puzzle is inconsistent. Checking parity consistency is a quick necessary condition before deeper search. The other options are not general invariants.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a puzzle where each profession allows only a subset of colours, what propagation technique removes a profession value when none of its allowed colours remain?

options.t: Support-count propagation from child to parent

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The hierarchy has parent attributes (profession) and child attributes (colour). Each profession value maintains a counter of currently supported colour values. When a colour is eliminated from a person's domain, the counters for professions that allowed that colour are decremented. If a profession's counter drops to zero, that profession value has no remaining support and is deleted from the domain. This bottom-up support-checking is analogous to arc consistency on the hierarchy edges and is more efficient than treating all profession-colour pairs as independent flat domains.

reasoning/puzzles.text: How should the conditional clue "If A sits at position 3 then B is a Doctor" be encoded in a SAT/SMT model?

options.t: As a permanent binary constraint between A's position and B's profession
As a global cardinality constraint on the number of doctors
As a parity constraint on the positions

reasoning/puzzles.sol: In SAT/SMT encoding, each possible assignment becomes a Boolean variable (e.g., x_A,3 for "A at position 3", y_B,Doctor for "B is Doctor"). A conditional clue is an implication that activates only when the antecedent holds. It is encoded as the clause (¬x_A,3 ∨ y_B,Doctor), which is logically equivalent to x_A,3 → y_B,Doctor. A permanent binary constraint would force the relation even when A is not at position 3, which is incorrect. Global cardinality and parity constraints address different aspects.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a multi-stage puzzle, three conditionals form a cycle: if A then B, if B then C, and if C then A. What does this cycle force about the truth values of the antecedents?

options.t: All three antecedents must be true
All three antecedents must be false
Either all three are true or all three are false
No definite conclusion can be drawn

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The three conditionals create a directed cycle in the implication graph. In Boolean logic, a cycle of implications (A→B, B→C, C→A) means A, B, and C are logically equivalent: each implies the others. Therefore they must share the same truth value. The only consistent assignments are all true or all false. Recognising this hidden equivalence lets the solver collapse the chain into a single binary choice, drastically reducing the search space.

reasoning/puzzles.text: A scheduling puzzle includes the clue "A and B cannot overlap". Before branching on the disjunction, which propagation technique can tighten the earliest and latest start bounds of the tasks?
reasoning/puzzles.sol: The non-overlap clue creates a disjunctive constraint: either A finishes before B starts or B finishes before A starts. Before case splitting, the solver applies edge-finding rules, which examine the cumulative resource profile and the relative ordering of tasks to deduce tighter bounds on start times. Edge-finding can prove that one of the two orders is impossible, thereby narrowing the temporal windows without explicit branching.

reasoning/puzzles.text: A double-row puzzle states "the two rows are mirror images". Which single anchoring constraint is sufficient to break the row-wise reflection symmetry?

options.t: Fix the rightmost person of the second row
Fix the leftmost person of the first row
Fix the middle person of both rows

reasoning/puzzles.sol: A mirror-image clue introduces a reflection symmetry that swaps the two rows while reversing left-right order. This symmetry has order 2. To break it, we must fix a variable that is not mapped onto itself by the reflection. Fixing the leftmost person of the first row selects a unique representative from each orbit of the group action, eliminating the duplicate solution branches caused by the row-swap symmetry.

reasoning/puzzles.text: In a hybrid seating-resource puzzle, after listing all feasible seat-person pairs from the seating sub-problem, what is the correct next step to verify resource feasibility?

options.t: Assign resources greedily to the highest-ranked persons
Build a bipartite graph between persons and resource units and compute a maximum matching
Ignore resource constraints and solve seating completely first
Randomly pair persons with resources until all capacities are filled

reasoning/puzzles.sol: The coupling clues link seats to resources, so resource assignment depends on which person occupies which seat. After obtaining the support matrix of feasible seat-person pairs, we construct a bipartite graph where persons are connected to resource units they are eligible for. Running a maximum-matching algorithm (e.g., Hopcroft-Karp) determines whether a perfect matching exists. If not, any seat-person pair that participates in no perfect matching is pruned, and the process iterates to a fixed point.

reasoning/puzzles.text: What is the direct consequence of failing to propagate the contrapositive of a conditional clue during puzzle solving?

options.t: Antecedents that should be false remain active

reasoning/puzzles.sol: A conditional "if X then Y" yields the contrapositive "if not Y then not X". When Y is proven false, the contrapositive forces X to be false. If this propagation is omitted, X stays marked as active (possible) even though it must be false. This leaves spurious antecedents in the implication graph, potentially triggering incorrect consequents later and expanding the search space with invalid branches.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: What was the day of the week on 26th January 1950?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: Reference: 1 Jan AD 1 was Monday. Odd days from 1 AD to 1949 = 1949 years. 1949/400 = 4 cycles of 400 years (0 odd days each) + 349 years. 349 years = 264 normal (1 odd day each) + 85 leap (2 odd days each) = 264+170 = 434 odd days ≡ 0 mod 7. Wait, more precisely: every 400 years has 0 odd days. 1600 to 1949 = 349 years. From 1600 to 1949: leap years = 349/4 - century correction. 349/4 = 87 leap years. Century years: 1700,1800,1900 (3 non-leap centuries). So leap years in 1601-1949 = 87-3 = 84. Normal years = 349-84 = 265. Odd days = 265×1 + 84×2 = 265+168 = 433 = 61×7 + 6 ≡ 6 odd days. So 1 Jan 1950 = Monday + 6 = Sunday. Actually, standard reference: 1 Jan 1950 was a Sunday. But the question asks 26 Jan 1950. From 1 Jan to 26 Jan = 25 days ≡ 4 odd days (25 mod 7 = 4). So 26 Jan 1950 = Sunday + 4 = Thursday.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: What is the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at 4:40?
If 28th March 2020 was a Saturday, what day was 28th March 2022?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: From 28 March 2020 to 28 March 2021 = 365 days (2020 is leap, but Feb is before March, so the extra day in 2020 doesn't count — 2020 was leap but Feb 29 is before March 28). Actually, careful: from 28 March 2020 to 28 March 2021: 2020-21 is not a full year in terms of leap day. The period includes Feb 2021 which is not leap. So 365 days = 1 odd day. From 28 March 2021 to 28 March 2022: 365 days = 1 odd day. Total odd days = 2. Saturday + 2 = Monday.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: Five friends A,B,C,D,E sit in a row facing north. A at left end. B immediate right of A. C two places right of B. D left of E. Who is at right end?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: A B _ C _. D left of E, so D then E at end. A B D C E. E at right end.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: In a queue, Ram is 8th from front and 12th from back. Total people?
Six people sit in a circle facing center. P between Q and R. S left of Q. T opposite S. Who opposite P?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: Order clockwise: S-Q-P-R-?-T. U fills remaining. Opposite P is U.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: A older than B. C older than A. D younger than B but older than E. Who is second youngest?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: C > A > B > D > E. Second youngest = D.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: In class of 40, Ravi ranks 5th from top. Rank from bottom?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: Rank from bottom = 40+1-5 = 36.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: Four people on floors 1-4. A on even floor. B above C. D on floor 1. Who on floor 3?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: D=1, C=2, B=3, A=4. B on floor 3.

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: In a line, every 3rd person gets prize. First prize at person 3. 10th prize at which position?
Five books: Math left of Science. English right of Science. History left of Math. Geography between Math and Science. Middle book?

reasoning/calendar-clock.text: A taller than B, shorter than C. D shorter than E, taller than C. Second tallest?
reasoning/calendar-clock.sol: E > D > C > A > B. D is second tallest.

quant/number-system.text: If a number 774958A96B is divisible by 8 and 9, then find the value of (A + B).
quant/number-system.sol: For divisibility by 8, last three digits 96B must be divisible by 8. 96B is divisible by 8 when B = 0 or 8. For divisibility by 9, sum of digits must be divisible by 9. Sum = 7+7+4+9+5+8+A+9+6+B = 55+A+B. For A+B, try B=0 => 55+A must be divisible by 9 => A=8 => A+B=8. Try B=8 => 63+A divisible by 9 => A=0 or 9 => A+B=8 or 17. The smallest unique sum is 9.

quant/number-system.text: What is the LCM of (2³ × 3 × 5²) and (2² × 3² × 7)?
quant/number-system.sol: LCM is the product of highest powers of all prime factors. Highest power of 2 = 2³, 3 = 3², 5 = 5², 7 = 7¹. Hence LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5² × 7.

quant/number-system.text: Find the remainder when 2⁴⁵ is divided by 7.
quant/number-system.sol: The cyclicity of 2 mod 7 is 3 (2¹≡2, 2²≡4, 2³≡1). Since 45 = 3×15, we have 2⁴⁵ = (2³)¹⁵ ≡ 1¹⁵ ≡ 1 mod 7. Remainder = 1.

quant/number-system.text: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 360. If one number is 60, find the other.
quant/number-system.sol: For two numbers, Product = HCF × LCM. So 60 × other = 12 × 360 => other = (12 × 360) ÷ 60 = 4320 ÷ 60 = 72.

quant/number-system.text: What is the unit digit of (1234)¹⁰² + (5678)⁵⁸?
quant/number-system.sol: Unit digit depends only on unit digit of base. 4¹⁰²: Cyclicity of 4 is 2 (4¹=4, 4²=16→6, 4³=64→4). Even power → unit digit 6. 8⁵⁸: Cyclicity of 8 is 4 (8¹=8, 8²=64→4, 8³=512→2, 8⁴=4096→6). 58÷4=14 remainder 2 → unit digit 4. So 6+4=10 → unit digit 0. So answer is 0.

quant/percentage.text: If A's salary is 20% less than B's salary, then B's salary is what percent more than A's salary?
quant/percentage.sol: Let B's salary = 100. Then A's = 80. B's salary more than A's = (20/80) × 100 = 25%.

quant/percentage.text: The population of a town increases by 10% annually. If the present population is 1,21,000, what was it two years ago?
quant/percentage.sol: Let P be the population two years ago. After 10% increase each year: P × 1.1 × 1.1 = 121000 => P = 121000 ÷ 1.21 = 100000.

quant/percentage.text: If 60% of (x - y) = 30% of (x + y), then what percent of x is y?
A number is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. The net change is:
quant/percentage.sol: Let the number be 100. After 20% increase: 120. After 20% decrease: 120 × 0.8 = 96. Net change = 4% decrease. Formula: a + b + ab/100 = 20 + (-20) + (20×-20)/100 = 0 - 4 = -4%.

quant/percentage.text: In an examination, a student scored 40% marks and failed by 30 marks. Another student scored 50% and got 20 marks more than the passing marks. Find the maximum marks.
quant/percentage.sol: Let max marks = M and passing marks = P. Student 1: 0.4M = P - 30. Student 2: 0.5M = P + 20. Subtracting: 0.1M = 50 => M = 500.

quant/profit-loss.text: A shopkeeper sells an article at a 20% profit. If he had bought it at 10% less and sold it for Rs. 30 more, he would have made a 40% profit. Find the cost price.
quant/profit-loss.sol: Let CP = x. SP = 1.2x. New CP = 0.9x. New SP = 1.2x + 30. New profit = 40% on new CP => 1.2x + 30 = 1.4(0.9x) = 1.26x => 0.06x = 30 => x = 500.

quant/profit-loss.text: Successive discounts of 20% and 10% are equivalent to a single discount of:
quant/profit-loss.sol: Let MP = 100. After 20% discount: 80. After 10% discount on 80: 80×0.9 = 72. Total discount = 28%. Formula: a + b - ab/100 = 20 + 10 - (20×10)/100 = 30 - 2 = 28%.

quant/profit-loss.text: A vendor sells goods at cost price but uses 900 grams instead of 1 kg. His profit percent is:
quant/profit-loss.sol: He pays for 900g but sells as 1000g. CP of 900g = SP of 1000g. Profit = (1000-900)/900 × 100 = 100/9 = 11.11%. Formula: Error/(True value - Error) × 100.

quant/profit-loss.text: A man sold two articles for Rs. 990 each. On one he gained 10% and on the other he lost 10%. Find his overall profit or loss percent.
quant/profit-loss.sol: CP1 = 990/1.1 = 900. CP2 = 990/0.9 = 1100. Total CP = 2000. Total SP = 1980. Loss = 20. Loss% = 20/2000 × 100 = 1%. When SP is same and profit% = loss%, there is always a net loss.

quant/time-work.text: A can do a work in 10 days, B in 15 days. They work together for 4 days, then A leaves. How many more days will B take to finish the remaining work?
A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours and another can empty it in 20 hours. If both pipes are opened together, how long will it take to fill the tank?
quant/time-work.sol: In 1 hour, fill pipe fills 1/12, empty pipe empties 1/20. Net work = 1/12 - 1/20 = (5-3)/60 = 2/60 = 1/30. Time to fill = 30 hours.

quant/time-work.text: A, B and C can do a work in 20, 30 and 60 days respectively. They work together. A gets Rs. 7200 as his share of wages. Find the total wages.
quant/time-work.sol: Efficiency ratio A:B:C = 1/20:1/30:1/60 = 3:2:1. A's share = (3/6) of total = 7200 => Total = 7200 × 6/3 = 14400. Wait: A's share = 3/(3+2+1) × Total = 3/6 × Total = 7200 => Total = 14400.

quant/time-work.text: A and B together can do a piece of work in 12 days. B and C together can do it in 15 days. A and C together can do it in 20 days. In how many days can A alone complete the work?
A can do a work in 12 days. B is 50% more efficient than A. In how many days can B alone do the same work?
quant/time-work.sol: Efficiency ratio A:B = 100:150 = 2:3. Time is inversely proportional to efficiency. So time taken by B = 12 × 2/3 = 8 days.

quant/speed-distance.text: A train 300 m long passes a platform 700 m long in 50 seconds. Find the speed of the train in km/h.
quant/speed-distance.sol: Total distance = train length + platform length = 300 + 700 = 1000 m. Time = 50 sec. Speed = 1000/50 = 20 m/s. Convert to km/h: 20 × 18/5 = 72 km/h.

quant/speed-distance.text: A man rows downstream 24 km in 4 hours and upstream 12 km in 6 hours. Find the speed of the stream.
quant/speed-distance.sol: Downstream speed = 24/4 = 6 km/h. Upstream speed = 12/6 = 2 km/h. Speed of stream = (Downstream - Upstream)/2 = (6-2)/2 = 2 km/h.

quant/speed-distance.text: A man covers half of the distance at 30 km/h and the remaining half at 20 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.
quant/speed-distance.sol: Let total distance = 2d. Time for first half = d/30, for second half = d/20. Total time = d/30 + d/20 = (2d+3d)/60 = 5d/60 = d/12. Average speed = 2d ÷ (d/12) = 2d × 12/d = 24 km/h.

quant/speed-distance.text: A thief is spotted by a policeman from 200 m away. The thief runs at 8 km/h and the policeman chases at 10 km/h. How far will the policeman have to run to catch the thief?
quant/speed-distance.sol: Relative speed = 10-8 = 2 km/h = 2×5/18 = 5/9 m/s. Distance to cover = 200 m. Time to catch = 200 ÷ (5/9) = 200 × 9/5 = 360 sec. Distance run by policeman = 10 km/h × 360 sec = (10×5/18) × 360 = (50/18)×360 = 50×20 = 1000 m.

quant/algebra.text: If x + 1/x = 5, find x² + 1/x².
If a + b + c = 0, find the value of (a²/bc) + (b²/ca) + (c²/ab).
If x = 2 + √3, find the value of x + 1/x.
If x² - 5x + 6 = 0, find the sum of squares of the roots.
quant/algebra.sol: For ax²+bx+c=0, sum of roots = -b/a = 5, product = c/a = 6. Sum of squares = (sum)² - 2(product) = 25 - 12 = 13.

quant/algebra.text: If a³ - b³ = 56 and a - b = 2, find ab.
quant/algebra.sol: a³-b³ = (a-b)(a²+ab+b²) = 2(a²+ab+b²) = 56 => a²+ab+b² = 28. Also (a-b)² = a²-2ab+b² = 4. Subtracting: (a²+ab+b²)-(a²-2ab+b²)=28-4 => 3ab=24 => ab=8.

quant/geometry-trigo.text: In a triangle ABC, angle A = 60° and angle B = 40°. Find angle C.
quant/geometry-trigo.sol: Sum of angles in a triangle = 180°. So C = 180 - (60+40) = 80°.

quant/geometry-trigo.text: If sin θ = 3/5, find the value of tan θ + sec θ.
The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 30 m away is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
Two circles of radii 5 cm and 3 cm intersect at two points. If the distance between their centres is 4 cm, find the length of the common chord.
quant/geometry-trigo.sol: For intersecting circles, the line joining centers is perpendicular bisector of common chord. Using right triangles: Let half chord = x. For circle 1: 5² = x² + d² where d is distance from center 1 to chord. For circle 2: 3² = x² + (4-d)². Subtracting: 25-9 = d²-(4-d)² => 16 = d²-(16-8d+d²) => 16 = 8d-16 => 8d=32 => d=4. Then x² = 25-16=9 => x=3. Chord length = 6 cm.

quant/geometry-trigo.text: In a ΔABC, if AB = AC and angle B = 50°, find angle A.
quant/geometry-trigo.sol: AB=AC so base angles B=C=50°. A = 180-(50+50) = 80°.

ga/indian-history.text: Which of the following features of the Harappan civilization indicates a centralized authority capable of mobilizing labor for public works, as mentioned in the lesson?

options.t: The presence of a deciphered royal inscription at Mohenjo-Daro
The Great Bath at Mohenjo-Daro and the use of uniform fired bricks
The discovery of monumental palaces with throne rooms
The existence of a standing army barracks in the citadel area

ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson explicitly states: 'The use of uniform fired bricks, the presence of granaries, and the Great Bath at Mohenjo-Daro indicate a centralized authority capable of mobilizing labor for public works.' Option B directly matches this textual evidence. Option A is incorrect because the script remains undeciphered. Option C is contradicted by the text which mentions 'little evidence for monumental palaces.' Option D is not mentioned in the lesson.

ga/indian-history.text: In the Early Vedic period, the assemblies known as sabha and samiti performed which function according to the lesson?

options.t: They functioned as judicial courts presided over by the rajan
They were religious bodies responsible for conducting yajnas
They provided checks on the rajan's authority as assemblies of elders and warriors
They served as revenue collection agencies for the tribal polity

ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson states: 'The sabha and samiti, assemblies of elders and warriors respectively, provided checks on the rajan's authority.' This directly supports option C. Option A is incorrect as they are not described as judicial courts presided by the rajan. Option B is wrong because yajnas were centered on fire sacrifices performed by priests, not these assemblies. Option D is not mentioned in the text.

ga/indian-history.text: According to the lesson, which statement accurately describes Ashoka's Dhamma and its propagation?

options.t: Ashoka's Dhamma was a sectarian Buddhist doctrine enforced through edicts in Pali language only
Ashoka's Dhamma emphasized social ethics and was propagated through inscriptions in Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts
Ashoka's Dhamma focused exclusively on the promotion of Brahmanical rituals and varna duties
Ashoka's Dhamma was a military code for the Mauryan army inscribed on pillar capitals

ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson states: 'Ashoka's Dhamma emphasized social ethics, non-violence, and religious tolerance, propagated through edicts inscribed in Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts across the empire.' Option B matches this description. Option A is incorrect because Dhamma was not sectarian Buddhist doctrine nor limited to Pali. Option C is wrong as it was not exclusively Brahmanical. Option D is incorrect as it was not a military code.

ga/indian-history.text: Based on the comparison table in the lesson, which architectural legacy is correctly attributed to the Vakataka dynasty?

options.t: Stone temples at Deogarh and the Sarnath Buddha sculpture
The Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal in Vesara style
The Ajanta caves (caves 16, 17, 19, 26) with mural paintings
The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram and Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram

ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson's comparison table explicitly lists 'Ajanta caves (chaityas and viharas) with mural paintings' under Vakataka Dynasty's Architectural Legacy. Option A describes Gupta legacy (Deogarh, Sarnath). Option B describes Chalukya architecture (Virupaksha at Pattadakal). Option D describes Pallava architecture (Shore Temple, Kailasanatha). Only option C matches the Vakataka entry in the provided table.

ga/indian-history.text: The lesson states that the Delhi Sultanate's administrative framework relied on the iqta system. What was the primary purpose of this system?

options.t: To establish a centralized bureaucracy with salaried officials appointed by the Sultan
To grant revenue assignments (iqta) to military nobles (muqtis) in lieu of salaries
To create a hereditary land tenure system for peasant cultivators
To organize a spy network for monitoring provincial governors

ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson explicitly states: 'The Delhi Sultanate's administrative framework relied on the iqta system, whereby revenue assignments (iqta) were granted to military nobles (muqtis) in lieu of salaries.' This directly corresponds to option B. Option A describes a salaried bureaucracy, which contradicts the 'in lieu of salaries' phrase. Option C refers to peasant land tenure, not military revenue assignments. Option D describes a spy network, which is not mentioned in the lesson's description of the iqta system.

ga/indian-history.text: In the Vijayanagara Empire, the provincial governors who held military and fiscal authority in return for a fixed tribute were known as:
ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson states that the kingdom was divided into mandalams governed by nayakas or mandaleshvaras, who held military and fiscal authority in return for fixed tribute. Subahdars were Mughal provincial governors, zamindars were revenue collectors under the Mughals and later British, and mansabdars were Mughal nobles. Therefore, the correct term for Vijayanagara provincial governors is nayakas.

ga/indian-history.text: The land tax (kudimai) in the Vijayanagara Empire was usually assessed at what proportion of the produce?
ga/indian-history.sol: According to the lesson, the kudimai (land tax) was usually assessed at one‑sixth of the produce. The Mughal zabt system later fixed revenue at one‑third after a ten‑year average, but the Vijayanagara rate was one‑sixth. The other fractions do not match the stated assessment.

ga/indian-history.text: In the Mughal mansabdari system, the sawar rank indicated:

options.t: Number of cavalrymen to be maintained

ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson explains that each mansabdar held a dual rank: zat (personal status and salary) and sawar (number of cavalrymen to be maintained). Thus, sawar specifically denoted the cavalry obligation, not salary, jagir size, or religious standing.

ga/indian-history.text: Which Governor‑General of India introduced the Doctrine of Lapse?
ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson notes that the Subsidiary Alliance was associated with Wellesley, while the Doctrine of Lapse was a policy of Dalhousie. Cornwallis is known for the Permanent Settlement, and Curzon for later administrative reforms. Hence, Lord Dalhousie introduced the Doctrine of Lapse.

ga/indian-history.text: The Surat Split of 1907 divided the Indian National Congress into which two factions?
ga/indian-history.sol: The lesson states that the Surat Split (1907) divided the Congress into Moderates and Extremists. The other pairs refer to later or different political groupings; the Muslim League was a separate organization formed in 1906, not a faction of the Congress.

ga/indian-history.text: Which land survey was used by the Vijayanagara Empire to assess revenue?
ga/indian-history.sol: The passage states that Vijayanagara revenue was assessed through a systematic land survey called kadamba, which classified soil fertility, irrigation, and crop type. The other options refer to Mughal (zabt, dahsala) or British (ryotwari) systems. Therefore kadamba is correct.

ga/indian-history.text: The Maratha levy known as chauth is best described as:

options.t: a tribute paid to the Mughals

ga/indian-history.sol: The text explicitly describes chauth as a negotiated protection levy that was often collected irregularly and varied by region, distinguishing it from a regular tax or customs duty. It was not a tribute to the Mughals. Therefore the correct description is a negotiated protection levy.

ga/indian-history.text: Which statement about the Bhakti and Sufi movements is accurate according to the passage?

options.t: They exhibited regional languages and social bases

ga/indian-history.sol: The passage warns against treating the Bhakti and Sufi movements as monolithic, noting that regional languages, theological orientations, and social bases differed sharply. Thus the accurate statement is that they exhibited regional languages and social bases. The other options contradict this nuance.

ga/indian-history.text: The Permanent Settlement of 1793, introduced by Lord Cornwallis, fixed land revenue permanently with which class?
ga/indian-history.sol: The Permanent Settlement of 1793, enacted under Lord Cornwallis, permanently fixed the land revenue demand with hereditary zamindars in Bengal, later extended to parts of Madras and Bombay. It did not involve ryots, village headmen, or merchant guilds as the primary revenue holders. Hence hereditary zamindars is correct.

ga/indian-history.text: What was the core feature of the nayankara system in the Vijayanagara Empire?

options.t: Hereditary land grants to Brahmins for religious services
Revenue territories granted to military chiefs for a fixed troop quota
Direct revenue collection by central officials without intermediaries
Trade monopolies given to merchant guilds for port revenue

ga/indian-history.sol: The nayankara system was a military-feudal arrangement where the king granted revenue-bearing territories called amaram to military chiefs (nayakas) in return for a fixed quota of troops. The nayakas had autonomy in local administration but were subject to periodic inspections and the obligation to supply soldiers. Option A describes brahmadeya grants, not nayankara. Option C contradicts the decentralized nature of the system. Option D refers to commercial policies, not the military-feudal structure.

ga/indian-history.text: What was the political outcome of the internal factionalism in the Bahmani Kingdom by the early 16th century?

options.t: It was annexed directly by the Mughal Empire in 1526
It fragmented into five independent sultanates by 1518
It merged with the Vijayanagara Empire after the Battle of Talikota
It continued as a unified state until the British conquest

ga/indian-history.sol: The Bahmani Kingdom weakened due to factionalism between Deccani and Afaqi nobles. By 1518, it had disintegrated into five successor sultanates: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, and Berar. The Mughal annexation occurred much later (late 17th century). The Battle of Talikota (1565) involved Vijayanagara and the Deccan Sultanates, not a merger. The kingdom did not survive as a unified entity until the British period.

ga/indian-history.text: Which statement correctly describes the nature of the Mughal mansabdari system?

options.t: Mansabdari ranks were hereditary and jagirs were permanently assigned to families
Mansabdari ranks were non-hereditary and jagir assignments were transferable
Mansabdars were paid only in cash and never received land assignments
The mansabdari system was introduced by the Bahmani sultans

ga/indian-history.sol: The mansabdari system was a centralised administrative and military framework where ranks (mansabs) were not hereditary; they were conferred by the emperor and could be increased, decreased, or revoked. Jagirs (revenue assignments) were transferable and reassigned periodically to prevent local power bases. Option A is incorrect because heredity was not a feature. Option C is wrong as mansabdars were primarily compensated through jagirs. Option D confuses the Mughal system with the earlier Bahmani administration.

ga/indian-history.text: How does the lesson text characterise the architectural design of the Taj Mahal?

options.t: It was designed exclusively by Persian architects with no Indian influence
It represents a synthesis of Persian design and Indian stone-carving traditions
It was built entirely by European architects employed by the Mughals
Its architecture follows the traditional South Indian temple style

ga/indian-history.sol: The text explicitly states that attributing the Taj Mahal's design solely to Persian architects neglects the significant contribution of Indian master builders and the synthesis of local stone-carving traditions. This indicates a blended Indo-Persian architectural style. Option A is the misconception the text warns against. Option C is historically inaccurate. Option D describes Dravidian temple architecture, which is unrelated to the Taj Mahal's Mughal style.

ga/indian-history.text: What was the fundamental difference between the Permanent Settlement and the Ryotwari system?

options.t: Both systems settled revenue directly with the cultivators
Permanent Settlement used zamindars as intermediaries; Ryotwari settled directly with cultivators
Ryotwari was implemented in Bengal while Permanent Settlement was in Madras
Both systems were introduced by Lord Wellesley in 1798

ga/indian-history.sol: The Permanent Settlement (1793, Bengal) fixed land revenue permanently with zamindars, who acted as intermediaries between the state and cultivators. The Ryotwari system (Madras, Bombay) settled revenue directly with the cultivators (ryots), eliminating intermediaries. Option A is incorrect because only Ryotwari was direct. Option C reverses the regions of implementation. Option D is wrong on both the governor-general (Cornwallis introduced Permanent Settlement) and the year (1793, not 1798).

ga/indian-polity.text: The Indian Constituent Assembly, after the partition of the country, consisted of how many members?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson states that after the Muslim League's withdrawal and the partition of the assembly, the Indian Constituent Assembly was reduced to 299 members. This figure is explicitly mentioned in the description of the Assembly's composition and its first sitting on 9 December 1946. The other numbers (389, 300, 315) are not supported by the text.

ga/indian-polity.text: Which of the following words is NOT part of the Preamble as described in the lesson?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson lists the key words of the Preamble as "Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic". The word "Federal" does not appear in that enumeration. Therefore, Federal is the correct choice as the word not included in the Preamble according to the provided material.

ga/indian-polity.text: The Supreme Court's interpretation of Article 21 was expanded to require a fair, just and reasonable procedure in which case?

options.t: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India

ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson explicitly mentions that the narrow view of personal liberty in A.K. Gopalan (1950) was overturned in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which held that the procedure established by law must be fair, just and reasonable, thereby reading due process into Article 21. The other cases deal with basic structure, President's Rule, or other matters.

ga/indian-polity.text: What is the maximum duration of the Lok Sabha unless dissolved earlier?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson's section on Parliament states the composition and term of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The standard constitutional term of the Lok Sabha is five years from the date appointed for its first meeting, unless dissolved sooner. This is a well‑known constitutional provision reflected in the lesson's description of parliamentary tenure.

ga/indian-polity.text: The doctrine of basic structure of the Constitution was first enunciated by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?

options.t: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)

ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson clearly identifies Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) as the case that established the basic structure doctrine, listing its components such as supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, and rule of law. Subsequent cases like Indira Nehru Gandhi and Minerva Mills reinforced the doctrine but did not originate it.

ga/indian-polity.text: Under which article does the Constitution vest residuary legislative powers in Parliament?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson states that residuary powers belong to Parliament under Article 248, a departure from the Canadian model where they rest with the provinces. Article 249 deals with Parliament's power to legislate on State List subjects in national interest, Article 250 concerns legislation during Emergency, and Article 251 addresses inconsistency between central and state laws on Concurrent List subjects. Therefore, the correct article is Article 248.

ga/indian-polity.text: According to the 44th Amendment, a proclamation of National Emergency must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within what period and by what majority?

options.t: Within one month by special majority
Within two months by simple majority
Within one month by simple majority

ga/indian-polity.sol: The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" and mandated that the proclamation be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a special majority. It also required the President to act on the written advice of the Cabinet. The other options incorrectly state the time limit or the type of majority required.

ga/indian-polity.text: What was the outcome of the Supreme Court's 2015 judgment on the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)?

options.t: It upheld the NJAC as constitutional
It restored the collegium and mandated a Memorandum of Procedure
It transferred judicial appointment power to Parliament

ga/indian-polity.sol: In the 2015 judgment, the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act, thereby restoring the collegium system for judicial appointments. The Court also directed the government to finalize a Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) in consultation with the Chief Justice of India to bring transparency to the collegium's functioning. The collegium was not abolished, nor was the NJAC upheld.

ga/indian-polity.text: After the 91st Amendment (2003), which of the following is the only exemption from disqualification under the Tenth Schedule?

options.t: A split of one‑third of the legislature party
A merger with another party agreed to by at least two‑thirds of the original party's members
Resignation of the member before the Speaker decides
The Speaker's decision being final and non‑reviewable

ga/indian-polity.sol: The 91st Amendment removed the provision that allowed a split of one‑third of a legislature party to avoid disqualification. Now, the sole exemption is a merger of the original party with another party, provided at least two‑thirds of the original party's members agree. Resignation does not automatically cure a pending disqualification, and the Speaker's decision remains subject to judicial review for mala fide or perversity.

ga/indian-polity.text: Under which Article does the President exercise discretion in appointing the Prime Minister when no party commands a clear majority in the Lok Sabha?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson states that the President's discretionary powers include the appointment of the Prime Minister when no party commands a clear majority (Art. 75). Article 74 deals with the Council of Ministers aiding the President, Article 76 concerns the Attorney General, and Article 77 relates to conduct of government business. Therefore, the correct provision is Article 75.

ga/indian-polity.text: What is the maximum period within which a Governor's ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature after its reassembly, failing which it lapses?
ga/indian-polity.sol: According to the lesson, an ordinance promulgated by the Governor under Article 213 must be laid before the State Legislature within six weeks of reassembly; otherwise it lapses. This mirrors the six‑week requirement for Presidential ordinances under Article 123. The other options (four, eight, ten weeks) are not mentioned in the constitutional scheme described.

ga/indian-polity.text: Which constitutional provision establishes the collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson explicitly mentions that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3). Article 74(1) deals with the President acting on ministerial advice, Article 78 concerns the Prime Minister's duty to furnish information, and Article 85 relates to sessions of Parliament. Hence, Article 75(3) is the correct answer.

ga/indian-polity.text: In the case of a Money Bill passed by a State Legislative Assembly, what is the maximum period within which the Legislative Council may recommend amendments?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson states that the Legislative Council can only recommend amendments to a Money Bill within 14 days; the Assembly has the final say. This mirrors the procedure for Money Bills at the Union level. The other periods (7, 21, 30 days) are not prescribed for this stage in the State legislative process.

ga/indian-polity.text: According to the 2018 Supreme Court judgment on the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi, the LG's discretionary powers are confined to how many excluded subjects?
ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson notes that the 2018 Supreme Court judgment limited the Lieutenant Governor's discretion to three excluded subjects (public order, police, and land) and mandated that any difference of opinion be referred to the President. Therefore, the correct number of excluded subjects is three.

ga/indian-polity.text: Which of the following correctly describes the scope of immunity under Article 105(2) of the Constitution?

options.t: Immunity extends to criminal offences for statements made in the House.
The Speaker's certificate shields a member from prosecution for statements made outside the House.
Members enjoy immunity from arrest in civil cases during the session and 40 days before and after it.
Immunity from legal proceedings for any vote given in Parliament is absolute and non‑justiciable.

ga/indian-polity.sol: Article 105(2) read with the Code of Civil Procedure grants Members of Parliament immunity from arrest in civil cases during the session and for 40 days before and after it. This immunity does not cover criminal offences; a member can be arrested for a cognizable offence, though the House must be informed. The Speaker's certificate under Article 105(2) is conclusive only for speeches made inside the House, not outside. While Article 105(2) also provides immunity from legal proceedings for anything said or any vote given in Parliament, the question asks for the specific civil‑arrest immunity, making option C the accurate statement.

ga/indian-polity.text: Which statement accurately distinguishes breach of privilege from contempt of the House?

options.t: Breach of privilege occurs only when a specific privilege is violated, while contempt covers any act obstructing the House even if no specific privilege is breached.
Contempt is a subset of breach of privilege and cannot exist independently.
The House cannot punish for contempt; only courts have that authority.
The Committee of Privileges has final authority to punish for contempt without House approval.

ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson explains that a breach of privilege arises when a particular privilege (e.g., freedom of speech) is violated. Contempt, however, is broader: it includes any act that obstructs the House in performing its functions, even if no specific privilege is breached. This distinction was highlighted in the Keshav Singh case (1965). The House itself decides on contempt, and the Committee of Privileges only examines complaints; the final decision rests with the House. Therefore, option A correctly captures the difference.

ga/indian-polity.text: According to the Supreme Court in R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970), the President's satisfaction under Article 123 is:

options.t: Justiciable only on the ground of mala fide exercise.
Subject to judicial review on the merits of the ordinance.
Reviewable only if the ordinance is re‑promulgated more than once.

ga/indian-polity.sol: In R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970), the Supreme Court held that the President's satisfaction to promulgate an ordinance under Article 123 is not immune from judicial scrutiny; it can be challenged only on the ground that the satisfaction was mala fide (i.e., exercised in bad faith). The Court did not open the merits of the ordinance to review, nor did it make the power non‑justiciable altogether. Repeated re‑promulgation was later deemed a fraud on the Constitution, but the specific ruling in Cooper limited review to mala fide. Hence, option B is correct.

ga/indian-polity.text: What is the current Supreme Court approach towards the maintainability of Public Interest Litigation (PIL)?

options.t: Any citizen may file a PIL on any matter without any threshold test.
The Court applies a threshold test of bona fide public interest before entertaining a PIL.
PIL can be filed only by a person who is directly affected by the issue.
The Court does not examine the motive or bona fides of the petitioner.

ga/indian-polity.sol: The lesson notes a common misconception that PIL is an unrestricted right. In practice, the Supreme Court now applies a threshold test to ensure that the petitioner is acting bona fide in the public interest, not for personal or political motives. This gatekeeping prevents frivolous or vexatious petitions. The Court does not require the petitioner to be directly affected (locus standi is relaxed), but it does scrutinize the genuineness of the public interest claimed. Therefore, option B reflects the correct judicial stance.

ga/indian-polity.text: What majority is required for the GST Council to take a decision?

options.t: Simple majority of the States present and voting.
Two‑thirds majority of the weighted votes of the Centre and States.
Three‑fourths weighted majority of the total votes of the Centre and States.

ga/indian-polity.sol: The GST Council's voting mechanism assigns a weightage of one‑third to the Centre and two‑thirds to the States collectively. Decisions require a three‑fourths (75%) majority of the weighted votes, not a simple majority of States. This super‑majority ensures broad consensus between the Centre and the States on tax matters. The lesson explicitly warns against confusing this with a simple majority. Hence, option C is the correct description of the required majority.

ga/indian-polity.text: The electoral college for the election of the President of India consists of which of the following?

options.t: Elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of Legislative Assemblies of all States only
Elected members of both Houses of Parliament, elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States, and elected members of Legislative Assemblies of NCT of Delhi and UT of Puducherry
All members of both Houses of Parliament and all members of Legislative Assemblies of States
Elected members of Lok Sabha, elected members of Rajya Sabha, and elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States only

ga/indian-polity.sol: Article 54 specifies the electoral college for Presidential election comprises elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States. Article 55 and the 70th Amendment Act, 1992 extended this to include elected members of Legislative Assemblies of NCT of Delhi and UT of Puducherry. Nominated members of Parliament and State Legislatures are excluded. Option B correctly captures this complete composition.

ga/indian-polity.text: Which of the following statements regarding the discretionary powers of the Governor of a State is correct?

options.t: The Governor can exercise discretionary powers in any matter he deems fit for the interest of the State
The Governor's discretionary powers are confined to specific instances listed in Article 163 and judicial pronouncements
The Governor acts at his discretion in all matters related to Centre-State relations
The Governor's discretionary powers are unlimited but subject to the President's approval

ga/indian-polity.sol: Article 163(1) states the Governor shall be aided and advised by the Council of Ministers except in so far as he is required to exercise his functions in his discretion. The Supreme Court in various judgments (e.g., Nabam Rebia, 2016) has held that discretionary powers are not unlimited but confined to specific constitutional provisions like reservation of bills for President's consideration (Art. 200), recommending President's Rule (Art. 356), and administering Union Territories as Administrator. Option B accurately reflects this constitutional limitation.

ga/indian-polity.text: Which of the following is a mandatory provision under the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act for Panchayats?

options.t: Devolution of all 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule to Panchayats
Reservation of not less than one-third seats for women in Panchayats at all levels
Direct election of the Chairperson of Panchayat at the district level by voters
Fixed tenure of five years for Panchayats without any provision for dissolution before expiry

ga/indian-polity.sol: Article 243D (inserted by 73rd Amendment) mandates reservation of not less than one-third of total seats for women (including SC/ST women) in Panchayats at all three levels. The devolution of subjects under Eleventh Schedule (Art. 243G) is left to State Legislatures (not mandatory). Chairperson at village level is elected as per State law; at intermediate/district level, elected by and from elected members (Art. 243C). Tenure is five years but can be dissolved earlier (Art. 243E). Only Option B is a mandatory constitutional requirement.

ga/indian-polity.text: In the context of the administration of the National Capital Territory of Delhi, which of the following statements is correct?

options.t: The Lieutenant Governor acts solely on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters
The Lieutenant Governor exercises executive authority on reserved subjects (public order, police, land) and can refer matters to the President
The Legislative Assembly of Delhi has exclusive legislative power over all entries in the State List and Concurrent List
The Chief Minister of Delhi is appointed by the Lieutenant Governor without any constitutional provision for Council of Ministers

ga/indian-polity.sol: Article 239AA (inserted by 69th Amendment) provides for a Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers for Delhi. The LG acts on aid and advice of Council of Ministers except on reserved subjects (public order, police, land) where LG exercises discretion. In case of difference of opinion, LG can refer matter to President (Art. 239AA(4)). The Assembly has power on State List and Concurrent List entries except reserved subjects. Option B correctly describes LG's powers and the referral mechanism to President.

ga/indian-geography.text: Which of the following correctly describes the three parallel ranges of the Himalayan Mountain System from north to south and the location of duns?

options.t: A. Himadri, Himachal, Shiwaliks; duns lie between Himachal and Shiwaliks
B. Himadri, Shiwaliks, Himachal; duns lie between Himadri and Himachal
C. Himachal, Himadri, Shiwaliks; duns lie between Himadri and Shiwaliks
D. Shiwaliks, Himachal, Himadri; duns lie between Shiwaliks and Himadri

ga/indian-geography.sol: The Himalayas comprise three parallel ranges: the northernmost Great Himalayas (Himadri), the middle Lesser Himalayas (Himachal), and the outermost Shiwaliks. Longitudinal valleys between the Lesser Himalayas (Himachal) and the Shiwaliks are called duns, with Dehra Dun as the prominent example. Option A matches this north-to-south sequence and dun location. Options B, C, and D either reverse the order or misplace the duns.

ga/indian-geography.text: Regarding the alluvium of the Northern Plains, which statement accurately distinguishes Khadar from Bhangar?

options.t: A. Khadar is older alluvium containing kankar; Bhangar is newer alluvium annually renewed
B. Khadar is newer alluvium in floodplains, light and sandy; Bhangar is older alluvium above flood level with kankar
C. Both Khadar and Bhangar are newer alluvium but Khadar has kankar
D. Both are older alluvium but Bhangar is annually renewed

ga/indian-geography.sol: The Northern Plains' alluvium is divided into Khadar (newer alluvium) found in active floodplains — light, sandy, and renewed annually by floods — and Bhangar (older alluvium) lying above flood level, characterized by calcareous concretions called kankar. Option B correctly states this distinction. Option A reverses the attributes, while C and D incorrectly describe both as same-age alluvium.

ga/indian-geography.text: The major rivers of the Deccan Plateau — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri — flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal. What geological feature causes this drainage pattern?

options.t: A. The Western Ghats block westward flow
B. The Deccan Plateau slopes gently eastward
C. The Eastern Ghats are higher than Western Ghats
D. The Narmada rift valley diverts rivers east

ga/indian-geography.sol: The Deccan Plateau, formed by Cretaceous basaltic lava flows, tilts gently eastward. This regional slope directs the major peninsular rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) toward the Bay of Bengal. The Western Ghats form the western escarpment but the eastward slope is the primary control. Option A describes a barrier, not the slope cause; Option C is factually incorrect (Western Ghats are higher); Option D refers to the Narmada rift which separates Central Highlands from Deccan, not the Deccan's internal slope.

ga/indian-geography.text: Which statement about Indian coal reserves is correct?

options.t: A. Gondwana coal is Eocene age, high in sulphur, found in Assam and Meghalaya
B. Tertiary coal is Permian age, constitutes 98% of reserves, found in Damodar valley
C. Gondwana coal is Permian age, constitutes 98% of reserves, found in Damodar, Son, Godavari, Mahanadi valleys
D. Both Gondwana and Tertiary coal are Permian age but Gondwana has higher sulphur

ga/indian-geography.sol: Gondwana coal (Permian period, 250–300 million years old) accounts for 98% of India's coal reserves and occurs in the Damodar valley (Jharia, Bokaro, Raniganj), Son valley (Singrauli, Korba), Godavari valley (Ramagundam), and Mahanadi valley (Talcher). Tertiary coal (Eocene, 50–60 million years old) is found in northeastern states (Assam, Arunachal, Meghalaya, Nagaland) and is high in sulphur. Option C matches these facts. Options A and B swap the age, sulphur content, and locations of the two coal types. Option D incorrectly assigns Permian age to both.

ga/indian-geography.text: India holds the world's largest reserves of thorium (about 25%). Where do these reserves occur and what is their role in India's nuclear programme?

options.t: A. Thorium reserves are largest in Jharkhand's Singhbhum belt; used in first stage PHWR
B. Thorium reserves are largest in monazite sands of Kerala and Odisha coasts; central to three-stage programme (PHWR → FBR → Thorium reactors)
C. Uranium reserves are largest in monazite sands; Thorium is in Cuddapah basin
D. Thorium reserves are largest in Rajasthan; used directly in first stage reactors

ga/indian-geography.sol: Thorium reserves, constituting about 25% of global reserves, occur in monazite sands along the Kerala and Odisha coasts. They are pivotal to India's three-stage nuclear power programme: Stage 1 uses Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR) fuelled by natural uranium; Stage 2 uses Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR) to breed plutonium; Stage 3 will use thorium-based reactors to utilise the vast thorium reserves. Option B correctly identifies the location (monazite sands of Kerala and Odisha) and the strategic role in the three-stage sequence. Option A misplaces thorium in Singhbhum (uranium belt) and assigns it to Stage 1. Option C confuses uranium with thorium locations. Option D mislocates reserves in Rajasthan and suggests direct first-stage use.

ga/indian-geography.text: What key change did the 2019 amendment to the Inter‑State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 introduce to address delays in adjudication?

options.t: It allowed states to directly approach the Supreme Court without tribunal intervention
It established a single standing tribunal with multiple benches and a strict three‑year timeline
It made tribunal awards advisory rather than binding on riparian states
It transferred all water dispute resolution to the Central Water Commission

ga/indian-geography.sol: The lesson states that the 2019 amendment introduced a single standing tribunal with multiple benches and a strict three‑year timeline for adjudication, aiming to reduce the decades‑long delays that characterised earlier tribunals. Option A is incorrect because Article 262 and the Act still require tribunal adjudication before Supreme Court review. Option C is wrong because awards remain final and binding. Option D is not mentioned; the Central Water Commission is not given dispute resolution authority.

ga/indian-geography.text: Which climatic phenomenon offset a weak El Niño signal to produce above‑normal monsoon rainfall in India during 2019?
ga/indian-geography.sol: The text explicitly mentions that a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) in 2019 contributed to above‑normal rainfall despite a weak El Niño signal. It also notes that the IOD can offset ENSO, citing 1997 and 2019 as examples. The Madden‑Julian Oscillation, Pacific Decadal Oscillation, and Southern Annular Mode are not referenced in the lesson as factors for the 2019 monsoon.

ga/indian-geography.text: According to the lesson, when were the agro‑climatic sub‑zone boundaries last revised to reflect shifts in long‑term climate normals?
ga/indian-geography.sol: The lesson includes a specific caution: "Treating agro‑climatic zones as static — sub‑zone boundaries are revised when long‑term climate normals shift (last revision 2019)." This directly indicates 2019 as the year of the most recent revision. The other years (2012, 2015, 2021) are not mentioned in connection with agro‑climatic zone boundary updates.

ga/indian-geography.text: Which joint venture company was formed in 2019 by three Central Public Sector Enterprises to acquire overseas critical mineral assets for India?
ga/indian-geography.sol: The text states: "Khanij Bidesh India Ltd. (KABIL), a joint venture of three CPSEs (NALCO, HCL, MECL), was formed in 2019 to acquire overseas mineral assets." The other options are not mentioned in the lesson. KABIL is specifically named as the vehicle for overseas acquisition of critical minerals such as lithium and cobalt.

ga/indian-geography.text: As per the NDMA guidelines of 2020, how many potentially dangerous glacial lakes in the Himalayan states of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, and Sikkim were identified for installation of automated water‑level sensors and early‑warning sirens?
ga/indian-geography.sol: The lesson states: "The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines (2020) mandate installation of automated water‑level sensors and early‑warning sirens at 47 identified potentially dangerous glacial lakes in Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, and Sikkim." This exact figure is given. The other numbers (37, 57, 67) do not appear in the context of glacial lake monitoring.

ga/indian-geography.text: Under the Inter‑State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, as amended in 2002, what is the maximum period prescribed for a tribunal to complete its hearings?
ga/indian-geography.sol: The 2002 amendment to the Inter‑State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 introduced a mandatory three‑year limit for tribunal hearings, after which the award must be submitted.
