options.t: A phylogeny with polytomies resolved using molecular clock assumptions and discrete trait data.
A fully resolved, ultrametric tree and continuous trait data evolving under a Brownian motion model.
A non-ultrametric tree with branch lengths proportional to substitution rates and categorical trait data.
A star phylogeny topology to ensure statistical independence of tip data without transformation.

biology/evolution.sol: Independent Contrasts (IC) transforms tip data into statistically independent contrasts between sister nodes. The method assumes trait evolution follows Brownian Motion (BM), where variance accumulates proportionally to time. This requires an ultrametric tree (tips equidistant from root) so branch lengths represent time. Contrasts are standardized by the square root of the sum of branch lengths (expected variance under BM). The method also requires a fully resolved tree (no polytomies) and continuous traits. Option B lists all necessary conditions: fully resolved, ultrametric tree, continuous traits, and BM model.

biology/evolution.text: In the Hawk–Dove game, a mixed evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) with proportion p = V/C of Hawks exists under which condition?
biology/evolution.sol: In the Hawk–Dove game the payoff matrix gives a mixed ESS only when the cost of injury C exceeds the resource value V. If V < C, fighting is too costly for Hawks to dominate, so negative frequency‑dependent selection maintains a stable polymorphism with Hawks at frequency V/C. When V ≥ C a pure Hawk strategy becomes an ESS. Therefore the mixed ESS exists precisely when V < C.

biology/evolution.text: Which pattern of morph frequency change characterises Rock‑Paper‑Scissors dynamics in side‑blotched lizards?
biology/evolution.sol: Rock‑Paper‑Scissors dynamics involve three strategies each beating one and losing to another, creating non‑transitive cycles. In Uta stansburiana the orange, blue and yellow throat morphs cycle in frequency over generations. This produces persistent oscillations rather than a stable equilibrium, fixation or random drift. Hence the hallmark of such dynamics is persistent oscillations in morph frequencies.

biology/evolution.text: Antagonistic pleiotropy is best described as:

options.t: A single gene influencing multiple traits with beneficial effects on all
A single locus affecting two traits in opposite directions
Two different loci each affecting a single trait

biology/evolution.sol: Antagonistic pleiotropy occurs when one locus has opposite effects on two traits — beneficial for one trait and deleterious for another. The classic example is the HbS allele, which confers malaria resistance (advantage) but causes sickle‑cell anaemia in homozygotes (disadvantage). This differs from simple trade‑offs that may involve multiple loci; the defining feature is a single locus with antagonistic effects on two traits.

biology/evolution.text: In mammals, the majority of epigenetic marks are:

options.t: Only transmitted through the paternal line

biology/evolution.sol: During mammalian gametogenesis and early embryogenesis most DNA methylation and histone modifications are erased and re‑established, resetting the epigenome each generation. Only a small fraction escapes this reprogramming and can be transgenerationally inherited. Therefore the bulk of epigenetic marks are reset each generation rather than being stably inherited or behaving like genetic mutations.

biology/evolution.text: Formation of a neo‑sex chromosome by fusion of an autosome to an existing sex chromosome results in:
biology/evolution.sol: When an autosome fuses to a sex chromosome, the newly added region ceases recombination. This initiates the same degenerative forces — Muller's ratchet, background selection, and hitchhiking of deleterious mutations — that acted on the original non‑recombining chromosome. Consequently, the degeneration process restarts on the neo‑sex chromosome, leading to gene loss and repeat accumulation over evolutionary time.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which of the following statements about the central nervous system is correct?

options.t: The brain is protected by two meningeal layers: dura mater and pia mater.
Cerebrospinal fluid is produced by the choroid plexuses in the ventricles.
The spinal cord lacks meningeal coverings.
The cerebrum is part of the brainstem.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson states that the brain and spinal cord are each surrounded by three meningeal layers (dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater) and that cerebrospinal fluid is produced by the choroid plexuses in the ventricles. Therefore, option B accurately reflects the text, while options A, C, and D contain factual errors regarding meningeal layers, spinal cord coverings, and brain subdivisions.

biology/human-control-systems.text: In the autonomic nervous system, which neurotransmitter is released by postganglionic sympathetic fibers onto adrenergic receptors?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: According to the lesson, sympathetic preganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors in ganglia, and the postganglionic fibers then release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors to mediate fight‑or‑flight responses. Thus, norepinephrine is the correct postganglionic sympathetic neurotransmitter acting on adrenergic receptors.

biology/human-control-systems.text: The Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase pump maintains the resting membrane potential by transporting how many ions per ATP hydrolyzed?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: The text explicitly describes the Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase as actively transporting three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions into the cell per ATP hydrolyzed, establishing the steep concentration gradients that underlie the resting membrane potential of approximately –70 mV. This stoichiometry matches option B.

biology/human-control-systems.text: During skeletal muscle contraction, binding of Ca²⁺ to troponin C causes which immediate effect?

options.t: Movement of tropomyosin away from myosin‑binding sites on actin
Release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Hydrolysis of ATP by the SERCA pump

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The sliding filament mechanism described in the lesson states that calcium binds to troponin C, producing a conformational shift that moves tropomyosin away from the myosin‑binding sites on actin, allowing cross‑bridge formation. This step precedes the power stroke and is distinct from calcium release, myosin ATPase activation, or SERCA‑mediated reuptake.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which muscle fiber type is characterized by high myoglobin content, oxidative metabolism, and high fatigue resistance?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: The comparison table in the lesson lists Type I (slow‑oxidative) fibers as having high myoglobin content, oxidative phosphorylation as the primary metabolism, and high fatigue resistance, making them suited for posture and endurance activities. The other fiber types have lower myoglobin, greater glycolytic reliance, and lower fatigue resistance.

biology/human-control-systems.text: In hippocampal CA1 neurons, which description correctly matches the Ca²⁺ threshold and the key enzymes activated during long‑term potentiation (LTP) versus long‑term depression (LTD)?

options.t: High Ca²⁺ activates protein phosphatases PP1/PP2B, producing LTD.
Modest Ca²⁺ activates CaMKII and the Ras‑ERK pathway, producing LTP.
High Ca²⁺ activates CaMKII and the Ras‑ERK pathway, producing LTP.
Low Ca²⁺ activates CaMKII, producing LTP.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: LTP requires strong postsynaptic depolarisation that relieves the Mg²⁺ block of NMDA receptors, allowing a large Ca²⁺ influx. This high Ca²⁺ concentration preferentially activates Ca²⁺/calmodulin‑dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) and the Ras‑ERK cascade, leading to AMPA‑receptor phosphorylation, insertion, and spine enlargement. In contrast, low‑frequency stimulation generates only a modest Ca²⁺ rise, which preferentially activates the protein phosphatases PP1 and PP2B (calcineurin). These phosphatases dephosphorylate AMPA receptors and promote their endocytosis, causing spine shrinkage and LTD. Therefore, the statement that high Ca²⁺ activates CaMKII and Ras‑ERK for LTP is correct.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which second‑messenger pathway is characteristically activated by Gαq‑coupled G‑protein‑coupled receptors (GPCRs)?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: Gαq subunits stimulate phospholipase C‑β (PLC‑β), which hydrolyses PIP₂ into inositol‑1,4,5‑trisphosphate (IP₃) and diacylglycerol (DAG). IP₃ triggers Ca²⁺ release from the endoplasmic reticulum, while DAG remains in the membrane and activates protein kinase C (PKC). This IP₃/DAG/PKC cascade is the hallmark of Gαq‑mediated signalling, distinct from the Gαs‑cAMP/PKA, Gαi‑inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, or Gα12/13‑Rho pathways. Hence, the IP₃/DAG → PKC option correctly identifies the Gαq pathway.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Regarding skeletal muscle fiber‑type plasticity, which statement accurately describes the roles of PGC‑1α and the calcineurin‑NFAT pathway?

options.t: PGC‑1α directly causes fast‑to‑slow fiber‑type switching without calcineurin‑NFAT.
Calcineurin‑NFAT drives oxidative remodeling while PGC‑1α only regulates mitochondrial biogenesis.
PGC‑1α drives oxidative remodeling but fiber‑type switching requires calcineurin‑NFAT activation.
Both PGC‑1α and calcineurin‑NFAT independently cause fast‑to‑slow switching.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: PGC‑1α is a transcriptional co‑activator that promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative enzyme expression, thereby driving an oxidative phenotype. However, the actual conversion of fiber‑type identity (e.g., fast‑glycolytic to slow‑oxidative) depends on the calcineurin‑NFAT signalling cascade, which is activated by sustained Ca²⁺ signals during low‑intensity, high‑duration activity. Calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT, allowing its nuclear translocation and transcription of slow‑type contractile protein genes. Thus, PGC‑1α provides the metabolic remodeling, while calcineurin‑NFAT is essential for the contractile protein switch. The correct description is that PGC‑1α drives oxidative remodeling but fiber‑type switching requires calcineurin‑NFAT activation.

biology/human-control-systems.text: In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the primary defect is best described as:

options.t: Decreased ADH synthesis in the hypothalamus.
Impaired aquaporin‑2 trafficking to the collecting‑duct apical membrane despite normal ADH levels.
Autoimmune destruction of the posterior pituitary.
Excessive water intake suppressing ADH release.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus results from renal resistance to antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH (vasopressin) binds to V2 receptors on principal cells of the collecting duct, triggering a cAMP‑PKA cascade that phosphorylates aquaporin‑2 (AQP2) vesicles, promoting their insertion into the apical membrane. In the nephrogenic form, ADH synthesis and release are normal, but mutations in the V2 receptor or AQP2, or acquired factors (e.g., lithium), prevent AQP2 trafficking or membrane insertion. Consequently, water reabsorption fails despite adequate ADH. This matches the description of impaired AQP2 trafficking with normal ADH.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which of the following correctly defines mechanical advantage in terrestrial limb locomotion and gives the typical Strouhal number range for efficient swimming?

options.t: Mechanical advantage = ground‑reaction‑force moment arm / muscle moment arm; Strouhal number 0.5–0.8.
Mechanical advantage = muscle moment arm / ground‑reaction‑force moment arm; Strouhal number 0.2–0.4.
Mechanical advantage = muscle moment arm × ground‑reaction‑force moment arm; Strouhal number 0.1–0.2.
Mechanical advantage = ground‑reaction‑force moment arm – muscle moment arm; Strouhal number 0.4–0.6.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: Mechanical advantage (MA) of a limb lever system is the ratio of the muscle moment arm (distance from joint centre to muscle line of action) to the ground‑reaction‑force moment arm (distance from joint centre to the point of ground force application). A higher MA favours force production, while a lower MA favours speed. The Strouhal number (St = frequency × amplitude / velocity) characterises the efficiency of oscillatory swimming; values between 0.2 and 0.4 are observed across diverse fish and marine mammals for optimal propulsive efficiency. Therefore, the option stating MA = muscle moment arm / ground‑reaction‑force moment arm and Strouhal number 0.2–0.4 is correct.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which receptor subtype is correctly matched with its signalling mechanism?

options.t: NMDA receptor – Gq protein – phospholipase C activation
GABAB receptor – Gi protein – activation of K+ channels and inhibition of Ca2+ channels
Muscarinic M2 receptor – Gq protein – IP3/DAG pathway
5-HT3 receptor – Gs protein – adenylyl cyclase stimulation

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The text states GABAB receptors are Gi-coupled, activating K+ channels and inhibiting Ca2+ channels. NMDA receptors are ionotropic cation channels, not G-protein coupled. Muscarinic M2 receptors couple to Gi, not Gq. 5-HT3 receptors are ionotropic cation channels, not Gs-coupled. Thus only option B matches the described mechanism.

biology/human-control-systems.text: In the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which level of negative feedback involves suppression of CRH and AVP synthesis?

options.t: Fast non-genomic feedback via membrane glucocorticoid receptors
Intermediate genomic feedback via FKBP5 and GILZ transcription
Slow feedback via suppression of CRH/AVP synthesis
Ultradian feedback via ACTH pulse frequency modulation

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson describes three feedback levels: fast non-genomic membrane GR actions, intermediate genomic GR-mediated transcription of FKBP5 and GILZ, and slow suppression of CRH/AVP synthesis. Option C directly matches the slow feedback level. Option A describes fast feedback, option B describes intermediate feedback, and option D is not a defined feedback level in the text.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which statement accurately reflects the multifactorial basis of muscle fatigue as described in the lesson?

options.t: Fatigue results exclusively from lactate accumulation in muscle fibres.
Fatigue involves inorganic phosphate, H+, reactive oxygen species, and reduced central drive alongside lactate.
Fatigue is primarily caused by ATP depletion without involvement of metabolic byproducts.
Fatigue originates solely from peripheral mechanisms with no central nervous system contribution.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson explicitly warns against attributing fatigue solely to lactate accumulation, noting the roles of Pi, H+, ROS, and central drive reductions. Option B correctly lists these multiple factors. Option A represents the misconception the lesson identifies. Option C incorrectly singles out ATP depletion. Option D incorrectly excludes central mechanisms, while the lesson includes central drive reductions.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which feature correctly characterises Kallmann syndrome according to the lesson?

options.t: It presents with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and normal olfaction.
It results from failed GnRH neuronal migration due to ANOS1/FGFR1 mutations, causing anosmia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
It is caused by excessive kisspeptin expression leading to precocious puberty.
It involves dopamine-dependent suppression of GnRH by hyperprolactinaemia.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson states Kallmann syndrome combines anosmia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and results from failed GnRH neuronal migration due to ANOS1/FGFR1 mutations. Option A incorrectly describes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and normal olfaction. Option C describes a mechanism opposite to the GnRH deficiency in Kallmann syndrome. Option D describes hyperprolactinaemia's mechanism, which is a separate condition.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which myokine or osteokine action is correctly described in the bone-muscle crosstalk section?

options.t: Irisin is released from bone and acts on muscle GPRC6A receptors to enhance insulin sensitivity.
Osteocalcin is released from bone matrix during resorption and acts on muscle GPRC6A to increase insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial function.
Myostatin promotes muscle hypertrophy and bone formation through Smad2/3 signalling.
Sclerostin enhances Wnt/β-catenin signalling to stimulate bone formation.

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson states osteocalcin is released from bone matrix during resorption and acts on muscle GPRC6A receptors to increase insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial function. Irisin is a myokine cleaved from FNDC5 in muscle, not bone. Myostatin inhibits muscle growth and bone formation via Smad2/3. Sclerostin inhibits Wnt/β-catenin signalling; its suppression enhances bone formation. Thus only option B is accurate.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A gene encoding the skeletal muscle Nav1.4 sodium channel produce which clinical disorder?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson states that loss‑of‑function mutations in SCN4A cause hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 2, whereas gain‑of‑function mutations produce hyperkalemic periodic paralysis and paramyotonia congenita. Dravet syndrome and Brugada syndrome are linked to neuronal (SCN1A) and cardiac (SCN5A) sodium channel mutations, respectively. Therefore, the disorder directly resulting from a gain‑of‑function SCN4A mutation is hyperkalemic periodic paralysis.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Continuous administration of GnRH leads to gonadotropin suppression by causing receptor desensitization; this principle is clinically exploited using which agents?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: The portal system delivers GnRH in pulses; continuous GnRH exposure desensitizes its G‑protein‑coupled receptors on gonadotrophs, suppressing LH and FSH release. Clinically, long‑acting GnRH agonists are used to achieve this sustained exposure and down‑regulate gonadotropins, whereas antagonists block the receptor acutely. Dopamine agonists inhibit prolactin, and somatostatin analogs suppress GH and TSH, not gonadotropins via GnRH desensitization.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Self‑renewal of skeletal muscle satellite cells requires asymmetric division and activation of which signaling pathway?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson explicitly mentions that satellite cell self‑renewal depends on asymmetric division and Notch signaling. While Wnt, MAPK, and PI3K/Akt pathways are involved in myogenic differentiation and proliferation, the text identifies Notch as the critical pathway for maintaining the satellite cell pool through asymmetric division.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Fictive locomotion recorded from an isolated spinal cord demonstrates that central pattern generators can produce rhythmic motor output in the absence of:
biology/human-control-systems.sol: Fictive locomotion refers to rhythmic ventral root activity generated by the spinal cord in vitro, without any sensory feedback or descending commands. The lesson states that fictive locomotion proves intrinsic rhythm generation by CPG circuits, indicating they do not require sensory input to produce the basic locomotor pattern. Supraspinal input is also absent in the isolated preparation, but the key experimental evidence highlighted is the independence from sensory drive.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which of the following is NOT listed as a primary molecular mechanism of endocrine‑disrupting chemicals (EDCs) in the lesson?

options.t: Direct agonism or antagonism at nuclear hormone receptors

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The lesson enumerates five mechanisms: (1) direct receptor agonism/antagonism, (2) modulation of steroidogenic enzymes, (3) alteration of hormone‑binding globulins, (4) epigenetic reprogramming, and (5) interference with hormone transport across barriers. Activation of voltage‑gated sodium channels is a feature of channelopathies, not a recognized mode of action for EDCs. Therefore, this option is not a primary EDC mechanism described.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which of the following neurotransmitter receptors functions as a ligand‑gated ion channel (ionotropic receptor)?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) is a pentameric cation channel that opens directly upon acetylcholine binding, making it a classic ionotropic (ligand‑gated ion channel) receptor. Muscarinic M1, dopamine D2, and GABA_B receptors are all metabotropic G‑protein‑coupled receptors (GPCRs) that signal via second messengers, not by forming an ion pore.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Cortisol exerts its fast negative feedback on the HPA axis through which mechanism?

options.t: Non‑genomic action via membrane glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid receptors
Genomic action via pituitary glucocorticoid receptors
Genomic action via hypothalamic glucocorticoid receptors

biology/human-control-systems.sol: Fast feedback occurs within minutes and is mediated by non‑genomic mechanisms involving membrane‑associated glucocorticoid receptors (GR) and mineralocorticoid receptors (MR). The intermediate and slow feedback loops are genomic, acting at the pituitary and hypothalamus respectively over hours to days. Increased CRH synthesis would enhance, not inhibit, the axis.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which hormone stimulates renal 1α‑hydroxylase activity to increase active vitamin D synthesis?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) up‑regulates the renal 1α‑hydroxylase enzyme (CYP27B1), promoting conversion of 25‑hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D. FGF23 suppresses this enzyme, while calcitonin and cortisol do not directly stimulate 1α‑hydroxylase.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is the primary pathology of which movement disorder?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: Degeneration of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway (substantia nigra pars compacta → striatum) reduces dopamine input to the basal ganglia, causing the classic hypokinetic syndrome of Parkinson’s disease. Huntington’s disease involves striatal GABAergic neuron loss, hemiballismus results from subthalamic nucleus lesions, and dystonia has heterogeneous etiologies.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Cochlear amplification of basilar membrane motion is produced by which cell type and motor protein?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: Outer hair cells (OHCs) express the voltage‑dependent motor protein prestin (SLC26A5), which undergoes conformational changes driven by membrane potential, causing OHC length changes (electromotility) that amplify basilar membrane vibrations. Inner hair cells are the primary sensory receptors and use TMC1/2 MET channels for transduction, not prestin.

biology/human-control-systems.text: The core central pattern generator for locomotion in the mammalian lumbar spinal cord operates as a half‑center oscillator. Which mechanism underlies the alternating activity of flexor and extensor interneuron pools?

options.t: A single pacemaker neuron driving both pools
Continuous sensory feedback from muscle spindles
Descending cortical drive initiating each step

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The half‑center oscillator model describes two mutually inhibitory interneuron pools (flexor and extensor). Each pool inhibits the other; when inhibition wanes, post‑inhibitory rebound depolarization triggers the next burst, producing alternating rhythm without a single pacemaker. Sensory feedback and descending drive modulate but are not required for the basic rhythm, as shown by fictive locomotion in isolated spinal cords bathed in NMDA and serotonin.

biology/human-control-systems.text: A sub‑anesthetic intravenous infusion of ketamine is used for treatment‑resistant depression. Ketamine’s rapid antidepressant action is most directly mediated by antagonism of NMDA receptors containing which subunit?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: Ketamine preferentially blocks NMDA receptors that contain the GluN2B subunit. GluN1 is an obligatory subunit present in all NMDA receptors and does not confer subtype selectivity. GluN2A‑containing receptors have distinct kinetics and pharmacology, while GluN3 subunits form atypical receptors with different properties. Clinical and experimental data link GluN2B antagonism to ketamine’s rapid antidepressant effects.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Which adipokine, secreted by adipose tissue, enhances peripheral insulin sensitivity and increases sympathetic tone in addition to its central appetite‑regulating effects?
biology/human-control-systems.sol: Leptin acts on hypothalamic receptors to suppress appetite, but it also improves insulin sensitivity in liver and muscle and raises sympathetic nervous system outflow to peripheral tissues. Adiponectin enhances insulin sensitivity but does not increase sympathetic tone. Resistin and TNF‑α are associated with insulin resistance and inflammation, opposite to the described actions.

biology/human-control-systems.text: During prolonged submaximal exercise, the primary factor that limits substrate availability and contributes to muscle fatigue is:
biology/human-control-systems.sol: In prolonged submaximal exercise, muscle glycogen stores become exhausted, limiting the supply of glucose‑6‑phosphate for glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. This substrate shortage reduces ATP production and forces reliance on less efficient fuels, directly causing fatigue. While Pi accumulation, ROS, and SERCA impairment affect contractile function and Ca²⁺ handling, they are secondary to the fundamental limitation of fuel availability.

biology/human-control-systems.text: Adult neurogenesis in mammals is confined to two canonical neurogenic niches. These are:

options.t: Subventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral ventricles and subgranular zone (SGZ) of the hippocampal dentate gyrus
Hippocampal CA1 region and cerebral cortex

biology/human-control-systems.sol: The SVZ generates neuroblasts that migrate via the rostral migratory stream to become olfactory bulb interneurons. The SGZ of the dentate gyrus produces granule cells that integrate into hippocampal circuitry over 4‑6 weeks. No other brain regions, including CA1, cortex, cerebellum, or the embryonic ventricular zone, sustain neurogenesis in adult mammals.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Why are the testes located in the scrotum rather than the abdominal cavity?

options.t: To protect them from mechanical injury
To maintain a temperature 2–3 °C lower than core body temperature for spermatogenesis
To facilitate the secretion of testosterone by Leydig cells
To allow direct drainage of sperm into the epididymis

biology/human-reproduction.sol: The lesson states that the testes reside in the scrotum where a temperature approximately two to three degrees Celsius lower than core body temperature is maintained, and this thermal gradient is essential for the progression of spermatogenesis. Core body temperature is too high for normal sperm production; thus the scrotal location provides the necessary cooler environment. The other options describe protective or anatomical functions but do not address the temperature requirement that is explicitly highlighted as essential for spermatogenesis.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which hormone produced by the Sertoli cells selectively suppresses FSH secretion without affecting LH?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: According to the text, FSH binds to receptors on Sertoli cells, stimulating the production of androgen‑binding protein and inhibin. Inhibin then selectively suppresses FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary, whereas testosterone exerts negative feedback on both GnRH and LH. Therefore, inhibin is the hormone that specifically reduces FSH while leaving LH relatively unchanged.

biology/human-reproduction.text: What is the approximate duration of the complete spermatogenic cycle from spermatogonia to mature spermatozoa in humans?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The lesson explicitly mentions that the entire cycle from spermatogonia to mature spermatozoa spans roughly 64 days in humans. This value is a standard figure for human spermatogenesis and is directly provided in the text, making 64 days the correct answer.

biology/human-reproduction.text: In which part of the female reproductive tract does fertilisation normally occur?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The section on fertilisation states "Fertilisation in the Ampulla," indicating that the ampulla of the fallopian tube is the usual site where the sperm meets the ovum. The isthmus is a narrower segment closer to the uterus, while the uterine cavity and cervical canal are not the typical sites of fertilisation.

biology/human-reproduction.text: What is the primary mechanism of action of a copper‑bearing intrauterine device (IUD)?

options.t: Thickening of cervical mucus to block sperm entry
Suppression of the LH surge to prevent ovulation
Release of copper ions that are toxic to sperm and ova and provoke a sterile inflammatory response impairing implantation
Inhibition of endometrial proliferation through systemic progestin

biology/human-reproduction.sol: The text describes copper‑bearing IUDs as releasing copper ions that are toxic to sperm and ova and provoke a sterile inflammatory response that impairs implantation. This mechanism is non‑hormonal and distinct from methods that thicken cervical mucus, suppress the LH surge, or act via systemic progestin. Therefore, the copper ion release and inflammatory response constitute the primary contraceptive action.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which hormone secreted by the blastocyst prevents luteolysis of the corpus luteum during early pregnancy?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The blastocyst begins secreting hCG as early as day 6 post‑fertilisation. hCG binds to LH/hCG receptors on the corpus luteum, preventing its luteolysis and sustaining progesterone and estradiol production until the luteal‑placental shift at 8‑10 weeks. Progesterone and estradiol are products of the corpus luteum, not the signal that maintains it, and LH is pituitary‑derived.

biology/human-reproduction.text: The "window of implantation" in a typical 28‑day menstrual cycle corresponds to which days?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: Progesterone induces the secretory transformation of the endometrium, up‑regulating integrins, glycodelin and LIF that create a receptive period lasting about four days. In a 28‑day cycle this window occurs approximately on days 20‑24, i.e. the mid‑luteal phase when the endometrium is maximally receptive to the blastocyst.

biology/human-reproduction.text: In a standard IVF cycle, the final maturation trigger is administered when at least how many follicles reach a diameter of ≥17 mm?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: Controlled ovarian stimulation is monitored by serial ultrasound and estradiol. The trigger (hCG or GnRH agonist) is given when three or more follicles have attained a mean diameter of ≥17 mm, ensuring an adequate cohort of mature oocytes for retrieval 34‑36 hours later.

biology/human-reproduction.text: According to current evidence cited in the lesson, which agent is preferred as first‑line ovulation induction in PCOS for higher live‑birth rates?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The lesson explicitly states that evidence favours letrozole over clomiphene for higher live‑birth rates in PCOS‑related anovulation. Letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, achieves superior ovulation and pregnancy outcomes compared with clomiphene, while metformin and gonadotropins are used in specific contexts but not as first‑line.

biology/human-reproduction.text: The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 permits surrogacy only for which group?

options.t: Indian heterosexual married couples with proven infertility

biology/human-reproduction.sol: The Act allows only altruistic surrogacy for Indian heterosexual married couples who have proven infertility. Commercial surrogacy is prohibited, and the law does not extend eligibility to foreign nationals, single women, or couples without documented infertility.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which molecular marker appears on the apical surface of luminal epithelial cells around day 20 of the menstrual cycle and serves as a ligand for osteopontin on the trophoblast?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The implantation window is defined by expression of integrin αvβ3 on luminal epithelium around day 20, which binds osteopontin on the trophoblast. LIF peaks mid‑secretory but is a cytokine, not a surface integrin. HOXA10/11 are transcription factors. Pinopodes are morphological protrusions. Therefore integrin αvβ3 is the correct marker.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which HLA molecule expressed by the trophoblast binds inhibitory receptors on uterine natural killer (uNK) cells to promote maternal‑fetal tolerance?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: Trophoblast lacks classical HLA‑A, ‑B, and ‑DR but expresses non‑classical HLA‑G, HLA‑E, and HLA‑F. HLA‑G binds inhibitory receptors ILT2, ILT4, and KIR2DL4 on uNK cells, dampening cytotoxic responses. HLA‑A, ‑B, and ‑DR are absent on trophoblast. Thus HLA‑G mediates tolerance.

biology/human-reproduction.text: During early embryonic development, which epigenetic event characterises the genome‑wide reprogramming that resets parental methylation patterns?

options.t: Global DNA demethylation followed by de novo methylation

biology/human-reproduction.sol: Early embryonic epigenetic reprogramming involves genome‑wide DNA demethylation after fertilisation, erasing parental methylation patterns, followed by de novo methylation during implantation. This resets the epigenome and establishes new imprints. Histone modifications and X‑chromosome changes occur but the hallmark is global DNA demethylation/remethylation.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which ovarian reserve biomarker can be falsely elevated in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) due to increased granulosa cell mass?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: Anti‑Müllerian hormone (AMH) is produced by granulosa cells. In PCOS, the expanded granulosa cell pool raises AMH levels, giving a falsely high estimate of ovarian reserve. FSH, inhibin B, and estradiol are not characteristically falsely elevated in PCOS. Hence AMH is the biomarker that can be misleadingly high.

biology/human-reproduction.text: A deletion in which AZF subregion of the Y chromosome is classically associated with Sertoli‑cell‑only syndrome?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The AZF region on Yq11.23 is divided into AZFa, AZFb, and AZFc. AZFa deletions encompass USP9Y and DBY and are classically linked to Sertoli‑cell‑only syndrome. AZFb deletions cause meiotic arrest, while AZFc deletions show variable phenotypes with possible sperm retrieval. Therefore AZFa deletion corresponds to Sertoli‑cell‑only syndrome.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which protein marker appears on the apical surface of luminal epithelial cells specifically during the implantation window?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The implantation window (days 6–10 post‑ovulation) is defined by the transient appearance of integrin αvβ3 on the apical membrane of luminal epithelial cells. LIF peaks at day 7 but is a secreted cytokine, not a surface marker. HOXA10 is a nuclear transcription factor regulating stromal decidualization. MUC1 is lost from the glycocalyx during receptivity rather than gained. Therefore, integrin αvβ3 is the hallmark apical surface marker of endometrial receptivity.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Extravillous trophoblasts express which HLA class I molecule that binds inhibitory receptors ILT2/ILT4 on uterine NK cells to promote maternal‑fetal tolerance?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: Extravillous trophoblasts uniquely express the non‑classical HLA‑G molecule. HLA‑G engages the inhibitory receptors ILT2 (LILRB1) and ILT4 (LILRB2) on uterine NK cells, dendritic cells and macrophages, suppressing cytotoxicity and inducing angiogenic cytokines such as VEGF and PlGF. Classical HLA‑A and HLA‑B are down‑regulated on trophoblasts to avoid CD8⁺ T‑cell recognition, while HLA‑DR (class II) is absent. Hence HLA‑G is the key tolerogenic ligand.

biology/human-reproduction.text: During pre‑implantation epigenetic reprogramming, global DNA demethylation occurs but imprinted loci remain methylated. Which protein complex protects these imprints?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: After fertilisation, the paternal genome undergoes rapid TET‑mediated demethylation, yet differentially methylated regions (DMRs) of imprinted genes escape erasure. The zinc‑finger protein ZFP57 recognises a methylated hexanucleotide motif within DMRs and recruits the co‑repressor TRIM28 (KAP1), which in turn attracts DNMTs and histone modifiers to maintain methylation. DNMT3A performs de‑novo methylation later, TET enzymes drive demethylation, and PRC2 deposits H3K27me3 but does not safeguard DNA methylation at imprints.

biology/human-reproduction.text: A complete absence of spermatozoa in the ejaculate (azoospermia) with failed testicular sperm retrieval is most strongly predicted by microdeletion of which Y‑chromosome region?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The azoospermia factor (AZF) regions on Yq contain genes essential for spermatogenesis. Large deletions encompassing AZFa or AZFb remove multiple genes (e.g., USP9Y, DBY in AZFa; RBMY, PRY in AZFb) required for early germ‑cell survival and meiotic progression, resulting in Sertoli‑cell‑only histology and zero sperm retrieval by TESE. AZFc deletions (including DAZ) often permit focal spermatogenesis and successful sperm retrieval. AZFd is not a standard clinical region. Therefore AZFa microdeletion best predicts complete retrieval failure.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Chronic low‑dose exposure to bisphenol A (BPA) in males reduces testicular testosterone synthesis primarily by down‑regulating which two steroidogenic proteins?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: BPA binds estrogen receptor‑β and androgen receptor with low affinity, yet chronic exposure suppresses Leydig‑cell steroidogenesis. It decreases expression of the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR), which mediates cholesterol transfer to the inner mitochondrial membrane, and of CYP17A1 (17α‑hydroxylase/17,20‑lyase), the enzyme converting pregnenolone to androstenedione. Reduced StAR limits substrate availability, while lowered CYP17A1 blocks the androgen‑producing pathway, together diminishing testosterone output. CYP19A1 (aromatase) and 5α‑reductase act downstream and are not the primary targets of BPA‑induced down‑regulation.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which enzyme is directly activated by bicarbonate and albumin during sperm capacitation to increase intracellular cAMP?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: During capacitation, bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) and albumin cooperate to activate soluble adenylyl cyclase (sAC). This enzyme synthesises cAMP, which then stimulates PKA. PLC and CatSper act downstream or in parallel but are not the primary target of bicarbonate/albumin.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Binding of spermatozoa to which zona pellucida glycoprotein triggers the acrosome reaction in humans?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: The acrosome reaction is initiated when the sperm binds to ZP3 (in humans ZP3 and ZP4 share the ligand function). ZP3 engages a G‑protein‑coupled receptor complex, activating PLC and the IP₃/DAG pathway that leads to Ca²⁺ release and exocytosis.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which of the following is highlighted as a major interpretation pitfall in ovarian reserve assessment?

options.t: AMH correlates linearly with chronological age
Antral follicle count (AFC) is completely operator‑independent
Low AMH equates to absolute infertility
Using a single AMH value without age context

biology/human-reproduction.sol: The text lists several pitfalls; the first is using a single AMH value without age context — a 30‑year‑old with AMH 1.0 ng/mL has a different prognosis than a 40‑year‑old with the same AMH. The other statements are misconceptions but not the specific pitfall described.

biology/human-reproduction.text: The most common Y‑chromosome microdeletion region in male infertility, associated with variable phenotypes and TESE success rates of 50–70 %, is:
biology/human-reproduction.sol: AZFc deletions (containing the DAZ gene cluster) are the most frequent Y‑microdeletions. They present with phenotypes ranging from oligozoospermia to azoospermia, and testicular sperm extraction retrieves sperm in 50–70 % of cases, enabling ICSI.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) establishes endometrial receptivity during the window of implantation by activating which signaling pathway?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: LIF is a member of the IL-6 cytokine family. It binds to its receptor (LIFR) which associates with the gp130 signal transducer. This complex activates Janus kinases (JAKs), leading to phosphorylation and activation of STAT3. The gp130/JAK/STAT3 pathway is essential for the transcriptional changes that render the endometrium receptive; LIF knockout mice fail to implant.

biology/human-reproduction.text: In preimplantation embryos, global DNA demethylation spares imprinted loci due to protection by which protein complex?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: During the wave of global DNA demethylation after fertilization, imprinted genes retain their methylation marks. The zinc finger protein ZFP57 recognizes methylated sequences at imprinting control regions and recruits the co-repressor TRIM28 (KAP1). This complex then attracts DNA methyltransferases and histone modifiers to maintain methylation and protect imprints from TET-mediated oxidation and replication-dependent dilution.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Fragmented mitochondria with low membrane potential in aged oocytes are targeted for mitophagy via which molecular pathway?
biology/human-reproduction.sol: Loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane. PINK1 phosphorylates ubiquitin and recruits the E3 ligase Parkin (PARKIN). Parkin ubiquitinates outer membrane proteins, creating a signal for autophagic adaptor proteins (e.g., OPTN, NDP52) to recruit the autophagy machinery. MFN2/OPA1 mediate fusion; DRP1/FIS1 mediate fission; AMPK/ULK1 initiate general autophagy but are not the specific mitophagy receptors for depolarized mitochondria.

biology/human-reproduction.text: Which maternal KIR / fetal HLA-C genotype combination at the maternal-fetal interface confers the highest risk for pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction?

options.t: Maternal KIR AA with fetal HLA-C2
Maternal KIR B with fetal HLA-C1
Maternal KIR AA with fetal HLA-C1
Maternal KIR B with fetal HLA-C2

biology/human-reproduction.sol: Uterine NK (uNK) cells express inhibitory KIR receptors. The KIR AA haplotype contains only inhibitory KIRs (e.g., KIR2DL1 specific for HLA-C2). When fetal extravillous trophoblasts express HLA-C2, engagement of inhibitory KIR2DL1 on uNK cells delivers a strong inhibitory signal. This suppresses uNK angiogenic function and impairs spiral artery remodeling, leading to poor placentation, pre-eclampsia, and growth restriction. KIR B haplotypes contain activating KIRs that counteract this inhibition.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes a key feature of Mesolithic adaptations in the Indian subcontinent as evidenced by the Bhimbetka rock shelters?

options.t: The rock art exclusively depicts agricultural activities and domesticated animals, reflecting a fully Neolithic economy.
Microlithic tools were absent at Bhimbetka, which instead yielded only large Acheulean handaxes and cleavers.
The rock art includes hunting scenes, dancing figures, and possible ritual motifs, marking the first clear expression of symbolic behaviour.
Mesolithic groups at Bhimbetka practiced intensive wet-rice cultivation and lived in permanent mud-brick settlements.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson text explicitly states: 'The appearance of rock art at Bhimbetka, depicting hunting scenes, dancing figures and possible ritual motifs, marks the first clear expression of symbolic behaviour in the subcontinent.' Option A is incorrect because the art depicts hunting, not agriculture, and the economy was a broad-spectrum hunting-gathering-fishing one. Option B is false because Bhimbetka is noted for dense concentrations of microliths, not Acheulean tools. Option D describes Neolithic features (wet-rice cultivation, mud-brick settlements) which appear later at sites like Mehrgarh, not at Mesolithic Bhimbetka.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: In the context of the Indus Valley Civilization, which of the following urban planning features is highlighted in the lesson as a distinctive characteristic?

options.t: Cities were built on a radial plan with streets radiating from a central temple complex.
The use of standardized baked bricks and a sophisticated drainage system connecting houses to street drains.
Residential areas were strictly segregated by caste, with separate quarters for each varna.
Fortifications were constructed exclusively using timber and mud, with no stone or brick components.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson text under '2.1 Urban Planning and Architecture' (though the detailed text is truncated, the standard IVC features described in UPSC syllabus and implied by the lesson structure include standardized bricks and drainage). The text mentions 'Urban Planning and Architecture' as a section. Standard knowledge confirmed by the lesson's focus: IVC cities used standardized baked bricks and had advanced drainage systems where house drains connected to street drains. Option A describes a later historical pattern (e.g., some medieval cities), not IVC's grid pattern. Option C imposes later varna system on IVC, which is anachronistic. Option D is incorrect because IVC fortifications used baked bricks and stone.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: According to the lesson, how did the introduction of iron technology in the Later Vedic period contribute to social stratification?

options.t: Iron tools enabled the clearing of dense forests in the Gangetic plains, leading to surplus agriculture that supported a hierarchical varna system with brahmanas and kshatriyas at the top.
Iron was used exclusively for ritual purposes, reinforcing the priestly monopoly over religious ceremonies.
The scarcity of iron ore forced communities into egalitarian sharing networks, preventing the emergence of social classes.
Iron technology was imported from Central Asia and remained under the control of foreign merchants, limiting its social impact.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson section '3.3 Iron Technology and Social Stratification' links iron technology to the clearing of the Gangetic plains' dense forests, which facilitated expanded agriculture and surplus production. This surplus supported population growth and the crystallization of the four-varna hierarchy (brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya, shudra) with brahmanas and kshatriyas dominating. Option B is incorrect because iron was primarily utilitarian (axes, ploughshares). Option C contradicts the text's emphasis on surplus leading to stratification. Option D is false; iron working developed indigenously in the subcontinent (e.g., at sites like Malhar).

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which statement best reflects the nature of Ashoka's Dhamma as described in the lesson?

options.t: Dhamma was a narrow sectarian doctrine promoting Buddhism as the state religion and persecuting other faiths.
Dhamma emphasized moral governance, social responsibility, and religious tolerance, propagated through edicts in Prakrit using Brahmi script.
Dhamma was primarily a legal code prescribing harsh punishments for crimes against the state and the monarchy.
Dhamma focused exclusively on the promotion of Brahmanical rituals and the reinforcement of varna duties.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: Section '5.2 Ashoka's Dhamma and the Expansion of Moral Governance' indicates that Ashoka's Dhamma was a broad ethical framework emphasizing moral governance, social responsibility (respect for elders, kindness to servants, non-violence), and religious tolerance ('honouring all sects'). It was propagated through edicts inscribed in Prakrit (the common language) using Brahmi script across the empire. Option A is incorrect because Ashoka explicitly supported all sects. Option C describes a legalistic penal code, not the moral suasion of Dhamma. Option D confuses Dhamma with later Brahmanical smriti literature.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The lesson attributes which of the following scientific achievements to the Gupta period mathematician-astronomer Aryabhata?

options.t: The invention of the decimal place-value system, the concept of zero, and a heliocentric approximation of planetary motion.
The discovery of the circumference of the earth and the law of gravity, predating Newton by a millennium.
The systematization of surgical procedures in the Sushruta Samhita, including cataract surgery and rhinoplasty.
The compilation of the Pancha-Siddhantika, a summary of five earlier astronomical treatises.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: Section '6.3 Gupta Administration, Science, Literature and Art' explicitly states: 'Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya (499 CE) introduced the concept of zero, the decimal place-value system, and a heliocentric approximation of planetary motion.' Option B attributes Newtonian physics to Aryabhata, which is anachronistic. Option C describes the Sushruta Samhita, which the text notes was 'systematized' in this period but is traditionally dated earlier and attributed to Sushruta, not Aryabhata. Option D describes Varahamihira's work (Pancha-Siddhantika), not Aryabhata's.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: According to the lesson, what is the significance of the micro-erosion analysis conducted on cupules at Daraki-Chattan?

options.t: It conclusively proves that figurative art in India dates back to 30,000 BP.
It suggests an antiquity exceeding 30,000 years for non-figurative symbolic modifications, though the result awaits wider replication.
It confirms that cupules were used as territorial markers by Gond and Bhil communities.
It establishes that cupules predate the Bhimbetka rock paintings by several millennia.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson explicitly states: 'Micro‑erosion analysis of cupules at Daraki‑Chattan has been proposed to suggest an antiquity exceeding 30,000 years, which would make them among the oldest known symbolic modifications in the subcontinent; this result awaits wider replication.' Option B accurately reflects this qualified finding. Option A is incorrect because the analysis concerns non-figurative cupules, not figurative art, and the result is not conclusive. Option C confuses the ethnographic parallels drawn for rock art sites generally with the specific cupule analysis. Option D makes a comparative claim about Bhimbetka not supported by the text.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) dates obtained from sediment covering painted surfaces at Pachmarhi indicate:

options.t: A maximum age of 9,500 years for the paintings themselves.
A minimum age of 9,500 ± 800 years for the overlying deposits, providing a terminus ante quem for the art.
A direct date of 9,500 BP for the pigment used in the paintings.
The exact age of the Mesolithic phase at Bhimbetka.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson states: 'Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) on sediment covering painted surfaces at Pachmarhi yields minimum ages of 9,500 ± 800 years for the overlying deposits.' Since the sediment covers the paintings, the deposit is younger than the art, giving a minimum age (terminus ante quem) for the art. Option A incorrectly states 'maximum age'. Option C is wrong because OSL dates the sediment, not the pigment directly. Option D incorrectly extrapolates Pachmarhi dates to Bhimbetka.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which of the following sets of rivers correctly constitutes the 'Sapta Sindhava' (seven rivers) defining the early Vedic ritual space in the Punjab, as per the lesson?

options.t: Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, and Yamuna
Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, and Sarasvati
Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sarasvati, and Ganga
Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej, Sarasvati, and Ghaggar

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson explicitly enumerates: 'The “Sapta Sindhava” (seven rivers) — Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, and Sarasvati — defines the early Vedic ritual space in the Punjab.' Option B matches this list exactly. Option A substitutes Yamuna for Sarasvati. Option C substitutes Ganga for Sutlej. Option D substitutes Ghaggar for Beas (and misorders).

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Kautilya's Arthashastra classifies intelligence operatives into five types. Which of the following correctly matches one type with its description as per the lesson?

options.t: Stationary spies (sthanika) — recruited from marginalized groups
Wandering spies (sancharaka) — embedded in administrative offices
Secret agents (gudhapurushas) — posing as merchants, ascetics, or entertainers
Technical operatives (yantra) — employing mechanical or coded means

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson lists: '(1) stationary spies (sthanika) embedded in administrative offices; (2) wandering spies (sancharaka) posing as merchants, ascetics, or entertainers; (3) secret agents (gudhapurushas) recruited from marginalized groups; (4) double agents (dvandva) turned from enemy ranks; and (5) technical operatives (yantra) employing mechanical or coded means.' Option D correctly matches 'technical operatives (yantra)' with 'employing mechanical or coded means'. Option A swaps sthanika and gudhapurushas. Option B swaps sthanika and sancharaka. Option C swaps sancharaka and gudhapurushas.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the water management system at Dholavira as detailed in the archaeological record?

options.t: The site relied exclusively on groundwater extraction through wedge-shaped brick-lined wells similar to those at Mohenjo-daro.
A series of 16 rock-cut reservoirs with a combined capacity of approximately 250,000 m³ were linked by stone-lined channels and check-dams to regulate seasonal runoff.
The Great Bath at Dholavira measured 12 m × 7 m × 2.4 m and was waterproofed using gypsum mortar, identical to the Mohenjo-daro structure.
Irrigation canals traced via satellite imagery at Dholavira follow the paleochannel of the Indus River, confirming direct Harappan control over the Indus drainage.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The text explicitly states that Dholavira had 'a series of 16 rock-cut reservoirs, together capable of storing an estimated 250,000 m³ of rainwater, are linked by a network of stone-lined channels and check-dams that regulate seasonal runoff from the surrounding catchment.' Option A describes Mohenjo-daro's wells, not Dholavira's system. Option C incorrectly attributes the Great Bath (which is at Mohenjo-daro) to Dholavira. Option D misidentifies the river system; the canals follow the Ghaggar-Hakra paleochannel, not the Indus.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Regarding the development of Sanskrit prosody, which statement correctly distinguishes the Rigvedic practice from the later Chandas-shastra of Pingala?

options.t: The Rigveda hymns employ the binary matrix (laghu/guru) combinatorics formally codified by Pingala in the 3rd century BCE.
The term 'chandas' in the Rigveda refers exclusively to the Gayatri meter, while Pingala expanded it to include Tristubh and Jagati.
The Rigvedic hymns exhibit a developed metrical practice, but the systematic codification of meters and the binary combinatorial matrix (prastara) are attributed to Pingala's later Chandas-shastra.
Pingala's Chandas-shastra (c. 3rd century BCE) is a direct commentary on the Rigveda Samhita, preserving the original accentuation rules lost in later recensions.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The text states: 'The Rigveda preserves the earliest systematic reflection on poetic meter... the Chandas-shastra attributed to Pingala (c. 3rd century BCE) later codifies these rules, but the Rigvedic hymns themselves already exhibit a co[ntinuity]...' This confirms that the Rigveda shows developed practice, while Pingala's work is the later codification including the binary matrix (prastara). Option A incorrectly attributes Pingala's binary matrix to the Rigveda itself (a listed trap). Option B misrepresents the scope of 'chandas' in the Rigveda. Option D falsely claims Pingala's work is a direct commentary on the Rigveda Samhita.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: According to the Arthashastra as referenced in the lesson, how was the Mauryan land revenue share (bhaga) determined?

options.t: It was fixed uniformly at one-sixth (1/6) of the produce for all cultivated lands across the empire.
It varied according to the fertility of the soil and the nature of the crop, as explicitly allowed by the Arthashastra.
It was assessed solely by the Samaharta based on the total sown area, without reference to soil quality.
It was collected exclusively in cash (karshapana) at a rate set by the Sannidhata for each janapada.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson explicitly lists as a trap: 'Assuming the Mauryan bhaga was a fixed 1/6 for all regions; the Arthashastra allows variation by soil fertility.' Therefore, the correct statement is that the bhaga varied according to soil fertility and crop nature. Option A reflects the common misconception (the trap). Option C incorrectly describes the assessment method and ignores soil quality. Option D is incorrect because the text does not state revenue was collected exclusively in cash or set by the Sannidhata.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which of the following numismatic developments is explicitly documented in the lesson as evidence for the political decline of the Gupta Empire?

options.t: The introduction of lead and potin coinage bearing the 'Ujjain' symbol to supplement the gold standard.
The replacement of the dynastic 'Garuda' emblem with the 'Peacock' motif on gold dinaras after Kumaragupta I.
The well-documented debasement of the gold dinara weight standard following the reign of Skandagupta.
The cessation of silver rupyaka minting and the exclusive use of copper alloy for imperial issues.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson explicitly states in the 'traps' section: 'Treating Gupta gold dinara weight as immutable; post-Skandagupta debasement is well documented.' This directly identifies the debasement of the gold dinara after Skandagupta as a documented numismatic proxy for political decline. Option A describes Satavahana coinage, not Gupta. Option B invents a motif change not mentioned in the text. Option D describes a cessation of silver minting not supported by the provided text.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The Naneghat inscription (c. 70 CE) is a primary source for understanding which aspect of Satavahana administration?

options.t: The administrative division of the empire into ahara and vishaya governed by amatya and mahamatra.
The fiscal policy regarding tolls (sulka) levied on specific commodities passing through the Naneghat pass.
The land grant procedure to Buddhist monasteries recorded in the donative portion of the inscription.
The genealogy and regnal years of the Satavahana kings from Simuka to Yajna Sri Satakarni.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The text states: 'Satavahana inscriptions at Naneghat (c. 70 CE) record the donation of a cave by Queen Naganika and list tolls (sulka) levied on merchandise passing the pass: 1 karshapana per cartload of textiles, 2 karshapana per load of iron, and a variable rate for spices.' It also lists as a trap: 'Overlooking the role of the Naneghat pass toll records as primary evidence for Satavahana fiscal policy.' This confirms the inscription's primary value for fiscal policy (tolls). Option A describes Mauryan administrative terms not linked to this inscription. Option C mentions the cave donation but the fiscal data is the highlighted primary evidence. Option D is not supported by the text regarding this specific inscription.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: According to the Arthashastra (2.12), the basic monetary measure for state revenue was the kārṣāpaṇa. What was its approximate weight and metal content as evidenced by punch‑marked coin hoards?
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson states that the weight standard most frequently encountered for punch‑marked coins is the kārṣāpaṇa of approximately 3.4 grams of silver, and the Arthashastra (2.12) describes this unit as the basic monetary measure for state revenue. The Mauryan rūpya (≈3.2 g silver) and Gupta dīnāra (≈8 g gold) are later, distinct standards. Copper punch‑marked pieces existed but were lighter, less standardized small change, not the primary kārṣāpaṇa standard.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The term śreṇi in the Mauryan and post‑Mauryan periods denoted a corporate body. Which of the following accurately describes its composition as per the lesson?

options.t: Exclusively merchant associations engaged in long‑distance trade
Artisans, merchants, professionals and service providers such as barbers
Only craft guilds of weavers and metalworkers

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson explicitly warns against assuming guilds were exclusively merchant bodies; it states they included artisans, weavers, and even service providers such as barbers. The Arthashastra (3.9) lists the śreṇi among sources of royal revenue, and the Sohgaura copper plate records a guild of oil‑pressers, confirming the diverse occupational base.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The fourth Buddhist council is a key milestone in sectarian divergence. Which ruler and location are correctly associated with it in the lesson?
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson lists as a common trap "Attributing the fourth Buddhist council to Aśoka instead of Kaniṣka, or placing it at Pāṭaliputra rather than Kashmir." Therefore, the correct association is Kaniṣka and Kashmir. The other options represent frequent misattributions.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Brahmadeya land grants under the Guptas involved a significant transfer of rights. What was the nature of this transfer according to the lesson?

options.t: Purely religious donations with no administrative change
Transfer of fiscal and judicial rights to the donee
Grant of cultivation rights only, with revenue retained by the state
Temporary leasehold subject to annual royal confirmation

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson states that treating brahmadeya grants as purely religious donations without recognizing the transfer of fiscal and judicial rights to the donee is a major error. It emphasizes that these grants transferred fiscal and judicial rights, marking a shift from centrally administered revenue to a decentralized, grant‑based agrarian order.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī is the foundation of Classical Sanskrit. Which statement correctly characterizes its methodological nature?

options.t: A descriptive grammar of the spoken Sanskrit of his time
A prescriptive, generative system for the sacred language (chandas)
A lexicon of Vedic roots with accent markings
A comparative grammar of Prākrit and Sanskrit dialects

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson explicitly warns against "Equating Pāṇini’s sūtras with a descriptive grammar of spoken Sanskrit; they are a prescriptive, generative system for the sacred language." It notes the Aṣṭādhyāyī distinguishes between the spoken bhāṣā and the sacred chandas through the chandas‑sūtra (6.1.1) and employs a meta‑language to derive all valid forms from a finite set of roots and affixes.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: According to Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts, which official was instructed to tour the country every five years to verify the practice of Dhamma?
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The edicts explicitly state that the Mahāmātras were ordered to “tour the country every five years” to ensure Dhamma was being followed. The Kumāra was the provincial governor, the Pradeśika administered the district, and the Grāmika headed the village; none of them are described as undertaking this quinquennial inspection.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The earliest Gupta religious monuments, dated to the reign of Chandragupta II, are the rock‑cut caves at which site?
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson identifies the rock‑cut caves at Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh) as the earliest Gupta monuments, dated to Chandragupta II (c. 380‑415 CE). The Dashavatara temple is a later structural temple, Sanchi is primarily Mauryan/early Buddhist, and Ellora belongs to a later period.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Statistical analysis of the Indus Valley sign inventory and entropy values suggests that the script is of which type?
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson notes that the sign inventory and statistical entropy point to a logo‑syllabic system, ruling out a purely alphabetic, purely logographic, or purely syllabic classification.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which statement accurately reflects the survival and regional distribution of Vedic śākhās?

options.t: All śākhās survive in equal numbers across India.
Only a handful of śākhās survive, and their regional distribution is highly uneven.
Śākhās were uniformly transmitted and written down during the Mauryan period.
Every region preserves a complete set of the four Saṃhitās.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson explicitly states that only a few Vedic śākhās have survived and that their regional distribution is highly uneven, making the second option the correct description.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The Saka era used for dating Western Kṣatrapa coins begins in which year?
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The lesson specifies that the Saka era (epoch 78 CE) appears consistently on Kṣatrapa coins, allowing precise absolute dating (e.g., year 150 = 228 CE). The Vikrama era starts in 58 BCE, while 320 CE and 3102 BCE are unrelated epochs.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which statement about the regional variation in Ashokan edicts is correct?

options.t: Kharosthi versions include additional passages on animal welfare not found in Brahmi texts.
The Kandahar bilingual inscription translates "Dhamma" as "Eusebeia" and "Dikaiosyne".
Southern edicts at Sannati are written entirely in early Kannada using Brahmi script.
Pillar Edicts use exclusively Magadhi Prakrit without any Sanskritisms.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The Kandahar bilingual inscription is explicitly mentioned in the lesson as translating "Dhamma" into Greek "Eusebeia" (piety) and "Dikaiosyne" (justice), showing diplomatic adaptation for Hellenistic audiences. Option A is incorrect because Kharosthi versions omit animal welfare passages, not add them. Option C is wrong because southern edicts retain Magadhi text with only a postscript in early Kannada, not entirely in Kannada. Option D is false because Pillar Edicts show higher Sanskritisms, not pure Magadhi. Thus B is correct.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: According to the Arthashastra, who was responsible for the maintenance of road segments passing through villages?

options.t: Royal engineers appointed by the central government
Merchant guilds using the trade routes

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The Arthashastra stipulates that the village headman (gramika) is accountable for the upkeep of the road segment passing through his jurisdiction, with fines levied for potholes or obstructions. Option A is not mentioned; maintenance was decentralized. Option B is incorrect; merchant guilds are not assigned this duty. Option D is wrong; the courier corps used the roads but did not maintain them. Therefore C is correct.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which scholar first explicitly defined zero as a number and prescribed rules for arithmetic operations involving it?
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta explicitly defined zero (shunya) as a number and gave rules for its arithmetic operations. Aryabhata used a place-value alphabetic numeral system without a zero symbol. Varahamihira's Panchasiddhantika summarized five astronomical treatises but did not introduce zero. The concept of zero as a number appears first in Brahmagupta, not Aryabhata. Hence B is correct.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: What evidence directly corroborates Roman trade at the port of Muziris mentioned in Sangam literature?

options.t: Discovery of punch-marked coins with Roman legends
Excavation of Mediterranean amphorae at Pattanam (identified as Muziris)
References to Roman embassies in the Pattuppattu
Inscriptions detailing trade treaties with Roman emperors

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: Sangam texts mention Yavana (Roman) ships at Muziris exchanging gold for pepper, and archaeology at Pattanam (identified as Muziris), Arikamedu, and Korkai has uncovered Mediterranean amphorae, corroborating this trade. Option A is unsupported; no Roman-legend punch-marked coins are mentioned. Option C is incorrect; the Pattuppattu contains poems but not references to Roman embassies. Option D is not mentioned; no inscriptions detailing trade treaties with Roman emperors are cited. Thus C is correct.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: Which feature of Satavahana urbanization is directly attested by an inscription at Nashik?

options.t: Construction of a grid-planned city layout
Donation of a water tank by Queen Naganika
Issuance of uniform gold coinage across the empire
Establishment of a centralized bureaucratic administration

mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The Nashik Cave 3 inscription records Queen Naganika's donation of a tank, directly evidencing royal involvement in hydraulic infrastructure. Option A is false: Satavahana cities grew organically around citadels and markets, unlike the Indus grid plan. Option B is contradicted by the documented debasement of lead coinage from high-lead to low-lead alloys. Option D is incorrect because the Amaravati stupa complex included monastic quarters, pilgrim rest-houses, and artisan workshops, forming a service economy, not a centralized bureaucracy. Therefore C is correct.

mains-gs1/ancient-india.text: The Baudhayana Sulba Sutra approximates the value of √2 as:
mains-gs1/ancient-india.sol: The Baudhayana Sulba Sutra provides an explicit fractional approximation for √2: 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3×4) − 1/(3×4×34). Evaluating this expression yields approximately 1.4142156, accurate to five decimal places. This demonstrates the advanced computational geometry embedded in Vedic altar construction.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: The Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) introduced in 1997 classified households into which categories based on a consumption-expenditure survey?

options.t: Above Poverty Line (APL) and Below Poverty Line (BPL) only
APL, BPL, and Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) categories
Priority and Non-Priority households under NFSA

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: The lesson states that the TPDS adopted in 1997 'classified households into Above Poverty Line and Below Poverty Line categories based on a consumption‑expenditure survey.' The AAY category was introduced later (2000) as a subset of BPL, and the three-fold APL/BPL/AAY classification became formalised under TPDS by 2000-01, but the 1997 launch specifically mentions only APL and BPL. The other options refer to later frameworks (NFSA's priority/non-priority) or design typologies (universal/categorical/means-tested) not used for the 1997 TPDS classification.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: Which of the following correctly describes the three targeting mechanisms discussed in the lesson's design principles section?
mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: Section 2.2 of the lesson is explicitly titled 'Targeting Mechanisms: Universal, Categorical and Means‑Tested' and discusses these three approaches. Universal targeting covers all residents (e.g., universal PDS pre-1997), categorical targeting uses group characteristics like age or occupation (e.g., pensions for elderly), and means-tested targeting assesses income/consumption (e.g., BPL lists). The other options represent different classification schemas not identified as the three core targeting mechanisms in the text.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: According to the lesson, what role did the Aadhaar biometric identity system play in the evolution of welfare delivery?

options.t: It replaced the need for social audits under MGNREGA and NFSA
It became the backbone of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) after being compelled by the rights-based framework
It was introduced as a conditionality requirement for receiving NFSA foodgrains
It served as the primary identification tool for the 1997 TPDS classification

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: The lesson states in section 1.3: 'The rights‑based framework also compelled the state to invest in identification infrastructure, most notably the Aadhaar biometric identity system, which later became the backbone of Direct Benefit Transfer.' This directly links Aadhaar to DBT architecture. Aadhaar did not replace social audits (they remain mandatory), was not a conditionality for NFSA (NFSA uses ration cards), and post-dates the 1997 TPDS which used consumption surveys.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: What is the correct coverage entitlement under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) as described in the lesson?

options.t: 75% of rural and 50% of urban population entitled to 5 kg per person per month
50% of rural and 75% of urban population entitled to 35 kg per household per month
Universal coverage for all citizens with 10 kg per person per month
Only BPL and AAY households covered with 7 kg per person per month

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: Section 1.3 states NFSA covers 'up to seventy‑five percent of the rural and fifty percent of the urban population.' Section 4.3 and the comparison table confirm the entitlement is '5 kg per person per month.' The Act also introduced portability (One Nation One Ration Card) and statutory accountability through State Food Commissions. Option B reverses the rural-urban percentages, Option C describes universal coverage (pre-1997 PDS), and Option D reflects the earlier TPDS/AAY framework with different quantities.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: Which governance reform mechanism is mandated under both MGNREGA and NFSA to empower gram sabhas to scrutinise expenditure and verify beneficiary lists?
mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: Section 5.3 explicitly states: 'Social audits, mandated under MGNREGA and NFSA, empower gram sabhas to scrutinise expenditure, verify beneficiary lists and demand corrective action.' This dual mandate is a key feature of the rights-based architecture. Outcome-based budgeting (section 5.2) is a central ministry tool, citizen engagement platforms are complementary digital tools, and performance-based grants are Finance Commission incentives to states - none are mandated for gram sabha-level scrutiny under both Acts.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the Supreme Court's 2018 ruling in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India regarding Aadhaar and welfare services?

options.t: Aadhaar must be made mandatory for all central and state welfare schemes.
Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for services that are not backed by law, and alternative identifiers must be provided.
Aadhaar authentication is optional only for Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) schemes.
Aadhaar is mandatory for all schemes except those explicitly exempted by the Finance Commission.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: The Supreme Court held that Aadhaar cannot be compelled for services lacking statutory backing. Consequently, the government introduced alternative identifiers such as voter ID and ration card for certain schemes. This ruling directly limits mandatory Aadhaar use and mandates provision of alternatives, making option B the accurate reflection of the judgment.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: Under the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), the cash benefit is conditioned on which specific health‑seeking behaviour?

options.t: Institutional delivery in a public or accredited private health facility.
Early registration of pregnancy within the first trimester.
Immunisation of the newborn within six weeks.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: JSY is designed to promote safe motherhood by providing cash assistance conditional on the beneficiary delivering in an institution (public or accredited private). The scheme does not require completion of antenatal visits, early registration, or newborn immunisation as the triggering condition; those are features of other programmes such as PMMVY. Hence, option B correctly identifies the JSY conditionality.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: What is the nature of the social audit requirement under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) and the National Food Security Act (NFSA)?

options.t: A one‑time audit conducted at the end of each financial year.
A mandatory periodic process that must be carried out at regular intervals.
An optional exercise left to the discretion of the Gram Panchayat.
A central government‑led audit with no role for local institutions.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: Both MGNREGA and NFSA institutionalise social audit as a recurring, mandatory exercise — not a single event. The legislation prescribes regular social audits (e.g., every six months under MGNREGA) to ensure continuous community oversight of implementation. Treating it as a one‑time or optional activity contradicts the statutory design. Therefore, option B accurately describes the mandatory periodic nature of social audits.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: For Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), what is the standard Centre‑State funding ratio for general category states?
mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: The lesson states that the typical funding pattern for CSS follows a 60:40 Centre‑State split for general category states, while special category states (North‑East, Himalayan) receive a 90:10 split. This ratio determines the fiscal space available to states for scheme implementation. Option B matches the prescribed 60:40 sharing arrangement.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.text: Which provisions were introduced by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 to govern data use in digital welfare delivery?

options.t: Mandatory Aadhaar linkage for all welfare databases and unrestricted data sharing.
Purpose limitation, data minimisation, and establishment of a Data Protection Board.
Removal of consent requirements for government agencies accessing citizen data.
Automatic deletion of all welfare data after one year.

mains-gs2/welfare-schemes.sol: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 brings in core data‑protection principles such as purpose limitation (data used only for specified purposes), data minimisation (collecting only what is necessary), and creates a Data Protection Board to oversee compliance.
