gs/governance-prelims.text: What is the consequence for a State that fails to report data on the Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF) for two consecutive quarters under a Centrally Sponsored Scheme?

options.t: The State's share in vertical devolution is permanently reduced by 1%
The central share for the subsequent quarter is withheld until compliance (fund-hold)
The scheme is converted from a 'core' to an 'optional' CSS for that State
The State is barred from accessing the Scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF), introduced by the Ministry of Finance in 2021, mandates quarterly reporting of output and outcome indicators on the PFMS and DM-CSS dashboards. The lesson explicitly states that States failing to report for two consecutive quarters face a 'fund-hold', where the central share for the subsequent quarter is withheld until compliance is achieved. This was evidenced in 2023 when five States experienced fund-holds under the National Health Mission due to delayed HMIS reporting. The other options describe consequences not mentioned in the text.

gs/governance-prelims.text: The 2022 Guidelines for Social Registry Data Quality issued by the Department of Rural Development mandate a minimum match rate between Aadhaar-seeded records and field-verified household surveys before a scheme can draw down funds. What is this prescribed minimum match rate?
gs/governance-prelims.sol: The lesson explicitly states: "The 2022 'Guidelines for Social Registry Data Quality' issued by the Department of Rural Development require a minimum 95 % match rate between Aadhaar-seeded records and field-verified household surveys before a scheme can draw down funds." This is a specific factual detail from the Unified Social Registry section. Options A, B, and D are incorrect percentages not mentioned in the text.

gs/governance-prelims.text: With reference to the evolution of performance budgeting in India, which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the Outcome Budget (2005-06) from the Performance Budget (2017-18)?

options.t: Outcome Budget introduced quarterly physical-financial reviews; Performance Budget linked funds to results for the first time.
Outcome Budget linked funds to results; Performance Budget added quarterly physical-financial reviews with Ministry of Finance, NITI Aayog's DMEO, and CAG.
Performance Budget replaced the Outcome Budget and removed the requirement for SDG-linked indicators.
Outcome Budget mandated gender-disaggregated data; Performance Budget extended this to disability-disaggregated data only.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The text states: "Performance budgeting in India evolved from the traditional line-item 'Demand for Grants' to a results-oriented framework beginning with the Outcome Budget (2005-06), followed by the Performance Budget (2017-18) and the integration of the PFMS... The Outcome Budget obliges each ministry to map every CSS to a set of output indicators... and outcome indicators... The Performance Budget adds a quarterly 'Physical-Financial Review' where the Ministry of Finance, NITI Aayog's DMEO, and the CAG jointly assess variance against targets." Option B accurately captures this sequential evolution and distinction. Option A reverses the roles. Option C is incorrect as Performance Budget did not replace Outcome Budget. Option D misstates the annexure requirements.

gs/governance-prelims.text: The lesson highlights a common misconception regarding Gender-Responsive Budgeting (GRB). Which of the following accurately describes the nature of GRB as per the lesson?

options.t: GRB operates as a separate budget head with dedicated fund allocations for women-centric schemes.
GRB is a tagging and reporting framework applied to existing allocations, requiring an intersectionality matrix disaggregating caste, disability, and minority status within gender tags.
GRB mandates that all centrally sponsored schemes allocate a minimum 30% of their budget to women beneficiaries.
GRB replaced the Gender Budgeting Statement and is now the sole mechanism for reporting gender-disaggregated data in the Outcome Budget.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The 'Common Misconceptions' section explicitly states: "Treating Gender-Responsive Budgeting as a separate fund — GRB is a tagging and reporting framework applied to existing allocations, not a new budget head." Further, the main text notes: "Gender Budgeting, Child Budgeting, and Disability Budgeting statements are now appended as annexures to the Outcome Budget, requiring sex-disaggregated, age-disaggregated, and disability-disaggregated data... Ignoring the intersectionality matrix in GRB reporting — ministries must disaggregate by caste, disability, and minority status within gender tags, not report aggregate women-only figures." Option B correctly synthesizes both points. Options A, C, and D describe features not supported by the text.

gs/governance-prelims.text: The 2018 Supreme Court judgment in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India had a specific impact on the mandatory use of Aadhaar for welfare schemes. What was the Court's ruling regarding Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016?

options.t: Struck down Section 7 entirely, prohibiting any mandatory Aadhaar linkage for welfare benefits.
Upheld Section 7 without modification, allowing mandatory Aadhaar for all central and state schemes.
Read down Section 7 to require that any mandatory Aadhaar linkage must be backed by a parliamentary law.
Delegated the authority to mandate Aadhaar linkage to the respective Ministry implementing the scheme.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The lesson states: "The 2018 Aadhaar judgment (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India) struck down Section 57 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016, which permitted private entities to demand Aadhaar authentication, and read down Section 7 to require that any mandatory Aadhaar linkage be backed by a parliamentary law." Option C accurately reflects this 'reading down' of Section 7. Option A is incorrect as Section 7 was not struck down. Option B is incorrect as the Court imposed a condition (parliamentary law). Option D has no basis in the judgment described.

gs/governance-prelims.text: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes a performance audit from a compliance audit as described in the CAG's mandate?

options.t: A compliance audit evaluates outcomes against predefined indicators such as person‑days generated or immunisation coverage.
A performance audit verifies adherence to rules, sanctions and procedures only.
A performance audit evaluates outcomes against predefined indicators and assesses whether the programme design is fit for purpose.
Both audits focus solely on financial regularity and do not examine programme outcomes.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The lesson states that a compliance audit verifies adherence to rules, sanctions and procedures, whereas a performance audit evaluates outcomes against predefined indicators — person‑days generated, calories delivered, immunisation coverage — and assesses whether the programme design itself is fit for purpose. Option C captures this distinction exactly. Options A and B reverse the roles, and option D incorrectly claims both audits ignore outcomes.

gs/governance-prelims.text: Under the One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC) scheme, which set of technical and administrative requirements must be satisfied for a beneficiary to lift subsidised foodgrains from any Fair Price Shop in the country?

options.t: Only a valid ration card issued by the home state.
Aadhaar seeding of the ration card, integration with the IM‑PDS platform, and functional POS devices at every FPS.
Registration on a central portal and approval from the Ministry of Consumer Affairs for each transaction.
A biometric verification at the home state FPS before any inter‑state purchase.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The lesson explains that ONORC operates on the Integrated Management of Public Distribution System (IM‑PDS) platform and requires the ration card to be seeded with Aadhaar, IM‑PDS integration across states, and functional point‑of‑sale (POS) devices at every Fair Price Shop. Option B lists all three mandatory conditions. Options A, C and D omit essential components or add non‑existent steps.

gs/governance-prelims.text: According to the 2020 PPP Guidelines mentioned in the lesson, which accountability mechanisms are mandatory for Public‑Private Partnerships in service delivery?

options.t: Only contractual penalties for non‑performance by the private partner.
Independent third‑party audit and citizen grievance redressal mechanisms.
Internal audit conducted by the private partner’s own audit team.
Annual financial audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General alone.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The lesson explicitly states that PPP accountability is not solely contractual; the 2020 PPP Guidelines mandate independent third‑party audit and citizen grievance mechanisms. Option B reflects this requirement. Options A, C and D describe narrower or incorrect mechanisms that do not satisfy the guideline’s mandatory provisions.

gs/governance-prelims.text: Which principle must any data‑sharing arrangement for welfare databases satisfy under the MeitY guidelines and the DPDP Act framework discussed in the lesson?

options.t: Data may be shared for any government purpose without further restriction.
The arrangement must satisfy the “purpose limitation” test.
The DPDP Act overrides the Aadhaar Act, allowing unrestricted sharing of biometric data.
No specific safeguards are required for welfare databases beyond basic encryption.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The lesson notes that any data‑sharing arrangement must satisfy the “purpose limitation” test, a frequent mains question topic. It also clarifies that the DPDP Act and the Aadhaar Act operate concurrently, not that one overrides the other. Option B correctly states the required principle, while options A, C and D misrepresent the legal framework.

gs/governance-prelims.text: The Behavioural Insights Team (BIT) – India, known as the Nudge Unit, was established under which institution and applies which analytical framework for redesigning citizen‑facing processes?

options.t: Ministry of Finance, using the COM‑B model exclusively.
NITI Aayog, using the EAST framework (Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely).
Prime Minister’s Office, using nudge theory without a structured framework.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, using default enrolment as the sole tool.

gs/governance-prelims.sol: The lesson states that the Nudge Unit was set up under NITI Aayog in 2020 and applies the “EAST” framework — Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely — to redesign citizen‑facing processes. Option B matches both the institutional home and the framework. Options A, C and D incorrectly identify the parent body or the analytical tool.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The Pitt's India Act of 1784 introduced a dual system of control over British India. Which of the following correctly describes this dual system?

options.t: A Board of Control in London for political matters and the Court of Directors for commercial functions
A Governor-General in Calcutta for administration and a Commander-in-Chief for military affairs
A Secretary of State in London for policy and a Viceroy in India for execution
A Parliamentary Committee for legislation and the East India Company for revenue collection

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states: "Pitt's India Act in 1784, which introduced a dual system of control: a Board of Control in London, responsible for political matters, and the Court of Directors, retaining commercial functions." Option A matches this description exactly. Option B describes a later administrative division. Option C describes the post-1858 structure under the Government of India Act. Option D is not mentioned in the text.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which of the following statements accurately distinguishes the Permanent Settlement of Bengal from the Ryotwari system?

options.t: The Permanent Settlement recognised zamindars as proprietors of land, while Ryotwari recognised the cultivator (ryot) as the direct proprietor
The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Madras Presidency, while Ryotwari was introduced in Bengal
The Permanent Settlement fixed revenue demand permanently, while Ryotwari fixed it for a period of 10 years
The Permanent Settlement was devised by Thomas Munro, while Ryotwari was devised by Lord Cornwallis

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson describes the Permanent Settlement as recognising zamindars as landlords/proprietors with fixed revenue demand. The Ryotwari system (associated with Thomas Munro in Madras) recognised the cultivator (ryot) as the direct proprietor with revenue settled directly with them. Option A correctly captures this distinction. Option B reverses the regions. Option C is incorrect because Ryotwari settlements were typically for 20-30 years, not 10. Option D reverses the architects: Cornwallis introduced Permanent Settlement, Munro was associated with Ryotwari.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The "drain of wealth" theory articulated by early Indian nationalists primarily referred to:

options.t: The unilateral transfer of Indian resources to Britain without adequate economic return
The decline of Indian textile exports due to British industrial competition
The extraction of land revenue exceeding the productive capacity of Indian agriculture
The outflow of bullion from India to pay for British military expenditures in China

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states: "The early leadership — Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji, and Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee — articulated the 'drain of wealth' theory and demanded a larger share of Indians in governance." This theory, developed by Naoroji, described the unilateral transfer of India's wealth and resources to Britain (through home charges, salaries, pensions, profits) without equivalent economic return. Option B describes deindustrialisation, a related but distinct phenomenon. Option C describes excessive land revenue demand. Option D is a specific component but not the comprehensive definition.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The Doctrine of Lapse, articulated by Lord Dalhousie in 1848, led to the annexation of several princely states. Which of the following states was NOT annexed under this doctrine according to the lesson?
mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson explicitly states: "The Doctrine of Lapse, articulated by Lord Dalhousie in 1848, further facilitated annexation by declaring that any princely state without a direct male heir would revert to Company control, leading to the absorption of Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur and Oudh." Mysore is not listed among the states annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. Mysore came under British influence after the defeat of Tipu Sultan in 1799 (mentioned in section 1.3) and was later restored to the Wodeyar dynasty under subsidiary alliance, not annexed via Doctrine of Lapse.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The Satyashodhak Samaj founded by Jyotirao Phule in 1873 differed from the Brahmo Samaj and Prarthana Samaj primarily in its:

options.t: Anti-caste, egalitarian ideology and focus on lower-caste mobilisation
Advocacy for widow remarriage and female education
Rejection of idol worship and promotion of monotheism
Emphasis on Vedic authority and shuddhi ceremonies

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states: "Phule's movement introduced a radical, anti-caste discourse that differed from the upper-caste led reform societies, and it laid the ideological foundation for later Dalit movements led by B.R. Ambedkar." The comparison table shows Satyashodhak Samaj's core ideology as "Anti-caste, egalitarian, education for lower castes" while Brahmo Samaj focused on "Monotheism, rationalism, anti-idolatry" and Prarthana Samaj on "Theistic reform within Hindu tradition". Option B describes campaigns common to multiple societies. Option C describes Brahmo Samaj. Option D describes Arya Samaj.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which Charter Act introduced competitive examination for entry into the covenanted civil service and separated the executive and legislative functions of the Governor‑General's council?
mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The 1853 Charter Act, passed after the Sikh wars, expanded the legislative council to twelve members and, crucially, opened the covenanted civil service to competitive examination based on the Northcote‑Trevelyan model. It also separated the executive and legislative functions of the council for the first time, requiring legislative business to be conducted in open sittings. The 1813 and 1833 Acts did not provide for competitive entry or executive‑legislative separation, while the 1861 Act came later and dealt with Indian representation.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: What did the 1858 Queen's Proclamation explicitly do regarding the doctrine of lapse?

options.t: Retained the doctrine of lapse with minor modifications
Extended the doctrine of lapse to all princely states
Replaced the doctrine of lapse with a new annexation policy

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The 1858 Queen's Proclamation, issued after the 1857 revolt, explicitly renounced the doctrine of lapse and promised to respect the "rights, dignity and honour" of the princes. This marked a shift from the Company's annexationist policy to a new paramountcy framework where the Crown became supreme suzerain while princes retained internal autonomy. The proclamation did not retain, extend, or replace the doctrine with another annexation policy.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which press legislation was repealed in 1881 and replaced by a milder registration act?

options.t: Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, enacted by Lord Lytton to curb nationalist criticism in Indian‑language newspapers, was repealed in 1881 under Lord Ripon. It was replaced by a milder registration act that required only registration of presses and did not impose the stringent pre‑censorship and security‑deposit provisions of the 1878 law. The other acts listed were either later or unrelated to the 1881 repeal.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: By 1885, approximately how many Indians had entered the Indian Civil Service (ICS)?
mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states that Indianisation of the ICS proceeded very slowly after the 1853 Charter Act introduced competitive examinations. By the time of the first Indian National Congress session in 1885, fewer than 30 Indians had succeeded in joining the covenanted civil service. This low number reflects the barriers of age limits, examination location in London, and cultural bias that persisted until the Aitchison Commission (1886) recommended reforms.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: According to Dadabhai Naoroji's "drain of wealth" thesis, which of the following was NOT identified as a channel of drain?
mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: Naoroji systematically articulated three channels of drain: (1) Home Charges — interest on Indian debt, pensions, and salaries of British officials paid from Indian revenues; (2) Trade Imbalance — forced export of raw cotton, opium, and indigo at low prices while importing manufactured textiles at high tariffs; (3) Remittances — private savings of European officers and merchants sent to Britain. Land revenue collection, though a heavy burden on peasants, was not listed by Naoroji as a separate drain channel; it was part of the fiscal system that financed Home Charges.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which of the following statements accurately distinguishes the Wood's Despatch (1854) from the Hunter Commission (1882)?

options.t: Wood's Despatch recommended vernacular primary education while the Hunter Commission opposed it.
Wood's Despatch established universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras; the Hunter Commission reviewed the implementation of the Despatch's recommendations.
The Hunter Commission introduced the 'payment by results' system; Wood's Despatch abolished it.
Wood's Despatch focused exclusively on technical education; the Hunter Commission shifted emphasis to literary subjects.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states that Wood's Despatch (1854) laid out a comprehensive framework including the establishment of universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857), grants-in-aid, and the principle of 'payment by results'. The Hunter Commission (1882) was constituted to review the implementation of Wood's Despatch. It highlighted neglect of primary education, over-emphasis on literary subjects, and low enrolment of girls and lower-caste children. Option A is incorrect because Wood's Despatch recommended vernacular primary education. Option C reverses the roles: 'payment by results' was introduced by Wood's Despatch. Option D is incorrect because Wood's Despatch did not focus exclusively on technical education; the Hunter Commission actually criticized the over-emphasis on literary rather than technical subjects.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879) was enacted primarily in response to which uprising?
mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson explicitly states: 'The Deccan Riots erupted in the Bombay Presidency when the Ryotwari settlement's rigid revenue demand coincided with a sharp fall in cotton prices after the American Civil War... The colonial response combined military repression with the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879), which restricted the alienation of land to non-agriculturists and capped interest rates — a rare instance of protective legislation prompted by unrest.' The Santhal Hul (1855-56) and Kol Rebellion (1831-32) occurred earlier and in different regions (Chotanagpur). The Pabna Peasant Uprising (1873-76) was in Bengal against zamindari oppression and did not lead to the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, which was specific to the Bombay Presidency's Ryotwari context.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Regarding the Ilbert Bill controversy, which statement reflects the final compromise as described in the lesson?

options.t: The Bill granted European and Indian judges equal jurisdiction without any safeguards for European defendants.
The compromise retained a provision for a jury of which at least half had to be Europeans, preserving European privilege.
The Bill was withdrawn entirely after European protests, leaving the existing racial jurisdiction intact.
Indian judges were given full powers to try Europeans, but only in districts with a majority Indian population.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson's 'common confusions' section states: 'Assuming the Ilbert Bill granted full equality; the compromise retained a jury provision that preserved European privilege.' The Ilbert Bill (1883) originally proposed to allow Indian judges to try European British subjects. Intense opposition from the European community led to a compromise: Indian judges could try Europeans, but the defendant could claim a jury, at least half of whose members had to be Europeans. This preserved racial privilege. Option A describes the original bill, not the compromise. Option C is incorrect as the bill was not withdrawn but amended. Option D is not mentioned in the lesson and misrepresents the compromise.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which of the following correctly describes the origin and nature of the first Famine Codes in British India?

options.t: The Famine Codes were formulated by the Famine Commission of 1901 and applied uniformly across all provinces from 1902.
The Strachey Commission (1880) produced the first Famine Codes, which were issued province-wise and often ignored in practice.
The Famine Codes emerged from the 1857 Revolt's aftermath and mandated gratuitous relief as the primary relief mode.
The Codes were a central legislation passed by the Imperial Legislative Council in 1880, binding on all provincial governments.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states: 'The Strachey Commission (1880) produced the first Famine Codes' and in the 'common confusions' section: 'Believing the Famine Codes were uniformly applied from 1880; they were issued province-wise and often ignored in practice.' The Famine Commission of 1901 was a later body (mentioned in confusions: 'Mixing up the Strachey Commission (1880) with the later Famine Commission (1901)'). The Codes were not a central legislation passed by the Imperial Legislative Council but administrative codes issued by provincial governments. They included 'test works' and gratuitous relief, but the lesson notes 'continued reliance on test works that excluded the most vulnerable', so gratuitous relief was not the primary mode.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Consider the following political associations: (1) British Indian Association, (2) Indian Association, (3) Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, (4) National Conference. Which sequence correctly orders them by year of foundation?
mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: From the lesson: British Indian Association (1851, Calcutta); Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870); Indian Association (1876, Calcutta); National Conference (1883, organised by Indian Association). Thus the chronological order is: 1 (1851) → 3 (1870) → 2 (1876) → 4 (1883). Option A matches this sequence. The lesson also notes in 'common confusions': 'Treating the Indian Association (1876) as the first all-India body; the British Indian Association (1851) and the National Conference (1883) preceded it.' This confirms British Indian Association (1851) came before Indian Association (1876). Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) falls between them. The National Conference (1883) was the last, organised by the Indian Association.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which of the following statements regarding the post-1857 reorganisation of the Indian Army is correct?

options.t: The Peel Commission (1859) recommended a ratio of one British soldier to three Indian soldiers.
The "martial races" doctrine was first codified in the Kitchener Reforms of 1902.
The Punjab Frontier Force, raised from 1849, became the model for selective recruitment based on the martial races theory.
The Bengal Army was retained intact after 1857 but its recruitment base was shifted to the Punjab.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The Peel Commission recommended a 1:2 ratio (British:Indian), not 1:3. The martial races doctrine was codified in the 1885 Recruiting Handbook, not the Kitchener Reforms (1902-09). The Bengal Army was disbanded after 1857, not retained. The text explicitly states: "The Punjab Frontier Force, raised from 1849, became the model for this selective recruitment; by 1885 it contributed over 30,000 men, predominantly Sikhs and Punjabi Muslims."

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: With reference to the "guarantee system" for railway construction in India (1849-1869), which statement is accurate?

options.t: It guaranteed a 5% annual return on paid-up capital to private companies, backed by the Government of India.
It continued unchanged until 1885, by which time the network reached 9,000 miles.
The system applied to state-built railways after 1869 under the State Railway Department.
It ensured a 5% return on total capital expenditure including government subsidies.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The text states: "The 'guarantee system' (1849-1869) attracted British private capital by promising a 5% annual return on paid-up capital, backed by the Government of India." The system was phased out in 1869, after which the State Railway Department took over construction. The guarantee applied only to private companies before 1869 and was on paid-up capital, not total capital expenditure.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: What was the status of the Indian rupee's monetary standard during the period 1835-1885 as described in the lesson?

options.t: The rupee was placed on a gold-exchange standard in 1835 following the Coinage Act.
The rupee remained on a silver standard throughout the period; the gold-exchange standard was adopted only in 1899.
The rupee operated on a bimetallic standard with fixed gold-silver ratio after 1857.
The Currency Act of 1861 formally adopted the gold-exchange standard for India.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson explicitly identifies a common error: "Assuming the rupee was on a gold-exchange standard before 1899; it remained a silver standard throughout the period." The gold-exchange standard was adopted later, in 1899. There is no mention of a Coinage Act in 1835 establishing gold standard, a bimetallic standard after 1857, or an 1861 Currency Act adopting gold-exchange standard.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Regarding Lord Ripon's Resolution of 1882 on local self-government, which of the following is correct?

options.t: It immediately introduced elected majorities in all municipal bodies across British India.
It applied only to the three Presidency towns of Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras.
Implementation varied, and many municipal bodies retained nominated majorities until the 1890s.
It was the same legislative measure as the Calcutta Municipal Act of 1876.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson lists as a common error: "Assuming Ripon's Resolution (1882) introduced elected majorities in all municipalities immediately; implementation varied and many bodies retained nominated majorities until the 1890s." It also notes the error of mixing the 1876 Calcutta Municipal Act with the 1882 Ripon Resolution. The resolution was not limited to presidency towns.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which of the following statements about the growth of the Indian jute industry in Bengal (1850‑1885) is correct?

options.t: The first power‑driven jute mill was established at Calcutta in 1850.
The Wellington Mill at Rishra began production in 1855.
By 1885, Indian merchants owned the majority of jute mill capital.
The 1881 Factory Act regulated all jute mills irrespective of size.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states that the first power‑driven jute mill, the Wellington Mill at Rishra, began production in 1855. The other options are contradicted: the first mill was not in Calcutta in 1850; capital ownership remained overwhelmingly British; and the 1881 Factory Act applied only to mills employing more than 100 workers, leaving many smaller units unregulated.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The commercial exploitation of the Raniganj coalfield accelerated after 1853 primarily because of:

options.t: The railway guarantee system creating demand for locomotive fuel.
Formation of the Jharia Coal Company.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The text explains that commercial exploitation accelerated only after the 1853 railway guarantee system created a guaranteed demand for locomotive fuel, and the opening of the East Indian Railway in 1855 linked Raniganj to Calcutta, cutting transport costs by 70 percent. The other options refer to later developments or unrelated factors.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 led to the establishment of High Courts in which three presidency towns?
mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson notes that the Indian High Courts Act 1861 created High Courts at the three presidency towns of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. The other combinations include cities that were not presidency towns at that time or were not part of the 1861 Act.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: During the 1857 revolt, the Calcutta‑Delhi telegraph line was cut by rebels, forcing the British to rely on couriers for critical weeks. This illustrates which aspect of the telegraph network?

options.t: Its strategic military purpose and vulnerability.
Its role in nationalist organisation from the outset.
Its exclusive use by British officers.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The passage highlights that the telegraph’s strategic military purpose dictated route selection and state funding, and its vulnerability was exposed when rebels cut the Calcutta‑Delhi line, compelling the British to use couriers. This demonstrates the network’s military role and its susceptibility to disruption, not its commercial or nationalist functions.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The dominant labour regime in the Assam tea industry until the 1920s was:

options.t: Indentured ‘coolie’ system recruiting migrants from Chotanagpur and Bengal.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson states that labour scarcity drove the adoption of the indentured ‘coolie’ system, recruiting workers from the Chotanagpur plateau and famine‑stricken Bengal districts. By 1885, 80 percent of the 350,000 tea workforce were indentured migrants, and the system persisted until 1920. The other options describe labour forms not used as the dominant regime in Assam tea gardens.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which of the following was a key feature of the Post Office Act of 1854 that aimed at administrative integration?

options.t: Introduction of a uniform postage rate of one anna for a half‑ounce letter anywhere in British India
Establishment of a separate postal service for princely states
Grant of exclusive mail‑carrying rights to private couriers
Creation of a centralised telegraph department under the Viceroy

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The 1854 Post Office Act placed the entire postal network under a single Director‑General and introduced a uniform postage rate of one anna for a half‑ounce letter throughout British India. This standardisation, together with prepaid stamps and free official mail, enabled rapid communication between the Viceroy’s secretariat and district collectors, thereby integrating administration. The other options describe arrangements that did not exist under the 1854 Act.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: What was the primary monetary consequence of the Currency Act of 1861?

options.t: It transferred the sole right of note issue from the Presidency Banks to the Government of India
It established the Reserve Bank of India as the central banking authority
It allowed joint‑stock banks to issue currency notes on a limited basis
It fixed the rupee’s exchange rate to the British pound sterling

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The Currency Act of 1861 withdrew the note‑issuing monopoly of the three Presidency Banks and vested the exclusive right of note issue in the Government of India. This move gave the colonial state direct control over the money supply but did not create a central bank; the Reserve Bank was founded only in 1935. The Act also did not permit joint‑stock banks to issue notes nor did it peg the rupee to sterling.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 is correctly associated with which of the following reforms?

options.t: Introduction of nominated non‑official members to the Governor‑General’s legislative council
Introduction of limited indirect elections for provincial legislative councils
Abolition of the distinction between official and non‑official members
Grant of full legislative powers to the Imperial Legislative Council

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The 1861 Act expanded the Governor‑General’s Executive Council for legislative purposes by adding nominated non‑official members, thereby providing a limited Indian voice in law‑making. It did not introduce any electoral principle; limited indirect elections were introduced only by the Indian Councils Act of 1892. The Act also retained the official majority and did not confer full legislative sovereignty.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Regarding the Indian Medical Service (IMS) during 1857‑1885, which statement is accurate?

options.t: Senior posts in the IMS remained reserved for British officers throughout this period
The IMS was fully Indianised by 1885 following the 1857 Revolt
Indian physicians were appointed as Surgeon‑Generals from 1862 onward
The IMS was merged with the Indian Civil Service in 1870

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson explicitly states that by 1885 the IMS employed over 30,000 Indians in subordinate roles while senior positions remained exclusively British until the 1920s. The service had been restructured in 1855 and 1862 for administrative efficiency, but Indianisation of the higher grades did not occur in this period. No merger with the Indian Civil Service took place.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: The rapid expansion of the Bombay cotton textile industry between 1854 and 1885 was primarily catalysed by which external event?

options.t: The American Civil War (1861‑65) which disrupted Confederate cotton supplies to Lancashire
The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 reducing freight costs
The Indian Tariff Act of 1879 imposing a 5 % duty on British yarn
The establishment of the Managing Agency system by European firms

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The American Civil War cut off Confederate cotton to British mills, creating a speculative boom in Indian cotton exports. Bombay merchants reinvested these export profits into mill construction, leading to the rise from one mill in 1856 to 58 mills by 1885. While the Suez Canal, the 1879 Tariff Act, and the Managing Agency system influenced the industry, the initial and decisive catalyst was the Civil War‑induced cotton shortage.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.text: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the Indian Forest Act of 1865 from the Forest Act of 1878?

options.t: The 1865 Act classified forests into Reserved, Protected, and Village categories, while the 1878 Act merely empowered the government to declare government forests.
The 1865 Act was a declaratory statute empowering the government to declare government forests, while the 1878 Act introduced the three-fold classification of forests.
The 1865 Act established the Dehra Dun Forest School for professional training, while the 1878 Act focused solely on revenue extraction from timber.
The 1865 Act extinguished all customary rights of tribal communities, while the 1878 Act recorded and protected existing rights in Protected Forests.

mains-gs1/modern-india-1757-1885.sol: The lesson explicitly states that the 1865 Act 'was largely a declaratory statute' empowering the government to declare any forest land as 'government forest', while 'real control came with the Forest Act of 1878' which 'classified forests into three categories: Reserved Forests, Protected Forests, and Village Forests'. Option A reverses the roles of the two Acts. Option C incorrectly attributes the Dehra Dun Forest School (established 1878) to the 1865 Act. Option D is incorrect because the 1865 Act did not extinguish rights; the settlement process under the 1878 Act 'recorded and often extinguished' rights in Reserved Forests, while Protected Forests had 'existing rights recorded'.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Under Article 74 of the Constitution, what is the extent of the President's discretion regarding the advice of the Council of Ministers?

options.t: The President may reject the advice outright and act independently.
The President must act on the advice but may require the Council to reconsider it once.
The President can act independently in all matters except financial bills.
The advice of the Council of Ministers is not binding on the President.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Article 74(1) mandates that the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Council of Ministers, making the advice binding. Article 74(2) provides a limited safeguard: the President may require the Council to reconsider its advice, but after such reconsideration the President must act in accordance with the advice tendered. Thus the President cannot reject the advice outright nor act independently; the only discretion is to send the advice back for a single reconsideration.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: How is the Vice‑President of India elected?

options.t: Directly by the people of India.
By an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament.
By the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
By the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Article 66 provides that the Vice‑President is elected by an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). The Vice‑President is not directly elected by the people, nor appointed by the President, nor elected by state legislatures. This electoral college reflects the federal character of the office while keeping it within the parliamentary framework.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: What change did the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) make regarding the President's ordinance‑making power?

options.t: Extended the maximum life of an ordinance to six months.
Provided that an ordinance cannot be promulgated when both Houses of Parliament are in session.
Removed the President's power to promulgate ordinances altogether.
Allowed the President to issue ordinances without the advice of the Council of Ministers.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The The 44th Amendment restored the pre-Emergency constitutional position. It reinstated the binding nature of ministerial advice under Article 74(1) and, under Article 123, provided that the President cannot promulgate an ordinance when both Houses of Parliament are in session. The six-week limit after Parliament reassembles is from the original Constitution (Article 123(2)), not a change made by the 44th Amendment; no longer period had been introduced by the 42nd Amendment.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) placed a ceiling on the size of the Union Council of Ministers. What is that ceiling?

options.t: 10 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
15 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
20 % of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
No ceiling; the size is determined by the Prime Minister.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A), which caps the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, at fifteen percent of the total number of members of the House of the People (Lok Sabha). This provision was introduced to prevent oversized cabinets and to promote administrative efficiency and fiscal discipline.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the creation of All‑India Services, and which body recruits them?

options.t: Article 320 – Department of Personnel and Training.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All‑India Services (such as the IAS, IPS and IFoS) common to the Union and the States. Recruitment to these services is conducted by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) through the annual Civil Services Examination. Central Civil Services, by contrast, are created under Article 309 and are recruited through separate examinations such as the Combined Graduate Level Examination.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: In the context of a hung Lok Sabha, which of the following statements accurately reflects the President's discretionary power and its judicial scrutiny as established in Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)?

options.t: The President must invite the leader of the single largest party and has no discretion to assess alternative claims.
The President's decision to dissolve the Assembly is immune from judicial review as it is based on ministerial advice under Article 74(1).
The President may refuse dissolution if advised by a caretaker government that has lost the confidence of the House, and such discretion is subject to judicial review for mala fide exercise.
The President is bound by a constitutional formula to invite the leader of the pre-poll alliance with the highest number of seats.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson states that in a hung Parliament, the President follows the convention of inviting the leader most likely to command a majority, but no constitutional formula exists. The 1996, 1998, and 1999 episodes show the President assessing competing claims. In Rameshwar Prasad (2006), the Supreme Court held that the President's decision to dissolve the Assembly is subject to judicial review for mala fide exercise. The Court reiterated that while the President acts on ministerial advice under Article 74(1), the advice must be constitutionally valid. If a caretaker government that has lost the confidence of the House advises dissolution, the President may refuse and explore alternative formations. Option A is incorrect because the President does have discretion to assess claims. Option B is incorrect because the decision is not immune from judicial review. Option D is incorrect because no constitutional formula exists.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Regarding the ordinance-making power of the President under Article 123, which principle was laid down by the Supreme Court in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)?

options.t: The President's satisfaction regarding the necessity of immediate legislation is entirely subjective and non-justiciable.
An ordinance can be repromulgated indefinitely without legislative approval as long as the President deems it necessary.
Repeated repromulgation of ordinances without legislative approval constitutes a fraud on the Constitution and an abuse of the ordinance-making power.
Ordinances lapse automatically after six weeks of Parliament's reassembly only if both Houses pass a resolution disapproving them.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson explicitly states that in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Supreme Court struck down a series of repromulgated ordinances, holding that repeated re-issuance without legislative approval constitutes a fraud on the Constitution and an abuse of the ordinance-making power. The ordinance must be laid before both Houses within six weeks of reassembly; otherwise it lapses. The President's satisfaction is not immune from judicial scrutiny. Option A is incorrect because the satisfaction is subject to judicial review. Option B is incorrect because indefinite repromulgation was held unconstitutional. Option D is incorrect because the ordinance lapses automatically after six weeks if not approved, not only if a disapproval resolution is passed.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Which of the following statements about Cabinet Committees in India is correct?

options.t: Cabinet Committees are statutory bodies established under an Act of Parliament.
The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) includes the National Security Adviser (NSA) as a permanent invitee.
The Cabinet Secretariat has no role in the functioning of Cabinet Committees.
Ad-hoc Groups of Ministers (GoMs) submit their recommendations directly to the Prime Minister, bypassing standing Cabinet Committees.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson states that Cabinet Committees are executive bodies under the Transaction of Business Rules, not statutory bodies. The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) is the apex security decision-making forum and includes the NSA as a permanent invitee. The Cabinet Secretariat provides secretarial support, minutes, and follow-up for these committees. Ad-hoc GoMs/EGoMs address cross-cutting issues and their recommendations feed into the appropriate standing Cabinet Committees, not directly to the Prime Minister bypassing them. Option A is incorrect because they are not statutory. Option C is incorrect because the Cabinet Secretariat provides essential support. Option D is incorrect because GoM recommendations feed into standing committees.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: In T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court issued directions to insulate civil services from political interference. Which of the following was NOT a direction given by the Court?

options.t: Establishment of a Civil Services Board at the Centre and in each state to recommend transfers, postings, and disciplinary actions.
Mandating fixed tenures for key posts such as Director General of Police and Chief Secretary.
Requiring that any premature transfer be recorded with reasons.
Making the Civil Services Board's recommendations binding on the political executive with no discretion to deviate.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson states that the Supreme Court in T.S.R. Subramanian (2013) directed the establishment of Civil Services Boards at the Centre and in states to recommend transfers, postings, and disciplinary actions; mandated fixed tenures for key posts like DGP and Chief Secretary; and required that any premature transfer be recorded with reasons. However, the lesson notes that the Centre's Civil Services Board functions largely in an advisory capacity, and compliance remains uneven. The Court did not make the Board's recommendations binding on the political executive with no discretion to deviate. Option D describes a direction that was not given.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Regarding Article 143 of the Constitution, which statement is correct?

options.t: The Supreme Court's advisory opinion is binding on the President and the Council of Ministers.
The President may refer only questions of fact, not questions of law, to the Supreme Court.
The advisory opinion is not binding but carries significant persuasive authority.
The Supreme Court is constitutionally compelled to answer every reference made by the President.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Article 143 empowers the President to refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion. The lesson explicitly states that the Court's advisory opinion is not binding on the President or the government, but it carries significant persuasive authority and has shaped executive action. The first reference in 1951 (Delhi Laws Act) and the 1998 Ayodhya reference illustrate this practice. The Court may also decline to answer a reference, as it did in the Ayodhya case. Hence, option C is the only accurate description.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) from the Cabinet Secretariat?

options.t: Both are constitutional bodies established under Article 74 of the Constitution.
The PMO is a constitutional‑administrative body, while the Cabinet Secretariat is a political office.
The PMO is a political office, whereas the Cabinet Secretariat is a constitutional‑administrative body.
The two offices are functionally interchangeable and share identical accountability mechanisms.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson highlights that the PMO is a political office serving the Prime Minister, while the Cabinet Secretariat is a constitutional‑administrative body responsible for inter‑ministerial coordination and recording Cabinet decisions. They have distinct origins, functions, and accountability structures; the PMO is not a constitutional body, and the Cabinet Secretariat is not a political office. The text warns against treating them as interchangeable. Therefore, option C correctly captures this institutional distinction.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Under the doctrine of pleasure (Article 310) and the safeguards of Article 311, which statement is accurate?

options.t: Article 311 protections apply to all civil servants from the date of recruitment, including probationers.
Article 311 protections apply only after a servant has been appointed to a substantive post, not during probation.
Parliament cannot modify the procedural safeguards of Article 311 through ordinary legislation.
The protections of Article 311 extend to employees of public sector undertakings and autonomous bodies.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson explicitly notes that Article 311 protections apply only after a servant has been appointed to a substantive post, not during probation. This is a key exception to the doctrine of pleasure under Article 310. Judicial expansion has added safeguards such as the right to be heard, but the threshold of substantive appointment remains. The protections do not automatically cover probationers, PSU employees, or autonomous body staff unless specifically extended. Hence, option B is the correct statement.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: What change did the Cadre Allocation Policy, 2017 introduce for All India Services officers?

options.t: It abolished the state‑cadre system and created a single national cadre pool.
It introduced a zone‑based allocation requiring officers to serve in at least one cadre outside their home zone.
It allowed officers to choose any state cadre solely on the basis of personal preference.
It removed the mandatory central deputation requirement for all AIS officers.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson states that the 2017 policy introduced a "zone‑based" allocation, dividing states into five zones and requiring officers to serve in at least one cadre outside their home zone to promote national integration. It did not abolish the cadre system, nor did it grant unrestricted choice or remove deputation requirements. The policy works within the existing cadre framework and the All India Services Act, 1951. Therefore, option B accurately reflects the 2017 reform.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: With reference to the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356, which of the following statements is correct?

options.t: The President's satisfaction is absolute and not subject to judicial review.
The proclamation must be approved by Parliament within one month.
The Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai mandated a floor test in the State Assembly within a reasonable time, preferably 48 hours, before imposition.
The dissolution of the State Assembly is a mandatory and routine sequel to the proclamation.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The S.R. Bommai (1994) judgment established that the President's satisfaction under Article 356 is subject to judicial review and is not absolute. The proclamation must be approved by Parliament within two months, not one. Crucially, the nine-judge bench mandated a floor test in the Assembly within a reasonable time, preferably 48 hours, before imposing President's Rule. Subsequent rulings in Rameshwar Prasad (2006) clarified that dissolution of the Assembly cannot be a routine sequel to the proclamation.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text:
Consider the following statements regarding the President's pardoning power under Article 72:
1. It is an absolute discretionary power of the President.
2. It is exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
3. It is immune from judicial review.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Article 72 power is not absolute; it is exercised by the President on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Statement 2 correct). The Supreme Court in cases like Maru Ram, Kehar Singh, and Epuru Sudhakar has held that this power is subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness, mala fides, and non-application of mind (Statement 3 incorrect). Therefore, Statement 1 is also incorrect as the power is not a personal discretion of the President.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: In the context of a minority government or a hung Parliament, which of the following accurately describes the President's discretion regarding the dissolution of the Lok Sabha?

options.t: The President is bound to dissolve the Lok Sabha immediately on the advice of the Prime Minister.
The President may refuse dissolution if a viable alternative government can be formed.
The President must refer the matter to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion before dissolving the House.
The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha only after a confidence motion is defeated on the floor of the House.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The President is not a mere rubber stamp regarding dissolution. While the President generally acts on ministerial advice, constitutional practice and judicial dicta recognize that the President may refuse dissolution if a viable alternative government exists and the House is not deadlocked. This discretion prevents the Prime Minister from using dissolution as a tool to avoid accountability when another ministry can command a majority. The President does not require a Supreme Court reference or a prior floor test defeat to exercise this discretion.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Which of the following statements about the 360-degree Performance Appraisal Report (PAR) under Mission Karmayogi is correct?

options.t: It applies to all civil servants from the level of Assistant Section Officer upwards.
It replaces the Annual Confidential Report (ACR) system for all Group A and Group B officers.
It applies only from the Under Secretary level upward, while lower-level officers continue under the older ACR system.
It is administered solely by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) without any role for the Capacity Building Commission.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Mission Karmayogi's 360-degree PAR is applicable from the Under Secretary level (Level 11) upwards. Officers below this level continue to be assessed under the traditional Annual Confidential Report (ACR) system. The Capacity Building Commission (CBC), not the DoPT, defines the competency framework and behavioural indicators for this appraisal. The PAR is conducted electronically on the iGOT platform covering six competency clusters.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: With reference to Financial Emergency under Article 360 of the Constitution, which of the following statements is correct?

options.t: It has been proclaimed once in 1991 during the balance of payments crisis.
During its operation, the President may direct the reduction of salaries of all persons serving in the State, including judges of the High Courts.
The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month.
The provision has never been invoked since the commencement of the Constitution.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Article 360 provides for Financial Emergency, but it has never been proclaimed in India's history, not even during the 1991 economic crisis. The proclamation must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate after two months unless approved by both Houses (not one month). While the President can direct reduction of salaries of persons serving the State, the constitutional protection of judges' salaries under Article 221 makes the inclusion of High Court judges in such a directive constitutionally contentious and untested.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: In B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), the Supreme Court held that the President's pleasure doctrine under Article 156 for removal of a Governor:

options.t: Is absolute and not subject to judicial review on any ground
Is not absolute; removal must not be arbitrary, mala fide or based on extraneous considerations
Requires prior consultation with the Chief Minister of the concerned state
Requires a resolution passed by the State Legislative Assembly

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The Supreme Court in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) explicitly ruled that the pleasure doctrine under Article 156 is not absolute. The Court held that removal of a Governor before completion of the five-year term cannot be arbitrary, mala fide, or based on extraneous considerations. The Court mandated that a removed Governor is entitled to a statement of reasons, and the decision is subject to judicial review for violation of constitutional morality. Option A is incorrect because the Court rejected absolute immunity. Option C is incorrect because while the Sarkaria Commission recommended consultation with the Chief Minister, this is not a constitutional requirement established by the judgment. Option D has no constitutional basis.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) derives its authority from:

options.t: A specific parliamentary statute enacted under Article 77
The executive's prerogative and the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules
A resolution of the Union Cabinet passed in 1947

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson text explicitly states: "Unlike other Cabinet committees, the CCS does not have a statutory basis; it derives its authority from the executive's prerogative." The CCS is chaired by the Prime Minister and comprises Ministers of Defence, Home Affairs, Finance, and External Affairs as permanent members. The National Security Adviser serves as its secretary. It is not established by a parliamentary statute (Option A), nor by a specific constitutional provision (Option C), nor by a 1947 Cabinet resolution (Option D). Its authority flows from the executive's prerogative to constitute committees for efficient transaction of business under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Regarding the Union Public Service Commission's role in disciplinary matters against civil servants, which statement is correct?

options.t: The UPSC's advice is binding on the President
The UPSC's advice is advisory, but non-consultation can invalidate the disciplinary order
The UPSC has no role in disciplinary matters; it only conducts recruitment examinations
The UPSC's advice is required only for Group A officers, not for Group B or C

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson's "Common Misconceptions" section explicitly states: "Believing the UPSC's advice in disciplinary matters is binding; it is advisory, though non-consultation can invalidate the order." Article 320(3)(c) of the Constitution requires the UPSC to be consulted on disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India. While the advice is not binding (Option A is incorrect), the Supreme Court has held that failure to consult the UPSC where mandated renders the disciplinary order void. Option C is incorrect because the UPSC has a constitutional role in disciplinary matters beyond recruitment. Option D is incorrect because the consultation requirement applies based on the nature of the penalty and service conditions, not merely Group classification.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: The post of Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister:

options.t: Is a constitutional authority created under Article 77
Is created by executive order and derives authority from the Prime Minister's discretion
Has a fixed tenure of five years as per the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules
Is appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson's "Common Misconceptions" section states: "Treating the Principal Secretary to the PM as a constitutional authority; the post is created by executive order and derives authority from the Prime Minister's discretion." The PMO itself is not a constitutional body but an executive creation to assist the Prime Minister. The Principal Secretary is typically a senior civil servant appointed by the Prime Minister, not through a constitutional process (Option A), not with a fixed statutory tenure (Option C), and not through the ACC appointment process which applies to certain senior posts like Secretary to Government of India (Option D). The post's authority flows entirely from the Prime Minister's delegation of functions.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: The Committee on Estimates differs from the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) in that:

options.t: The Committee on Estimates has 30 members from both Houses, while PAC has 22 members only from Lok Sabha
The Committee on Estimates examines proposed outlays for efficiency, while PAC audits past expenditure with the CAG
The Committee on Estimates can summon Ministers for evidence, while PAC can only call officials
The Committee on Estimates' reports are legally binding, while PAC's reports are only recommendatory

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson text clearly distinguishes: "Unlike the Public Accounts Committee (which audits past expenditure with the CAG), the Estimates Committee looks forward, evaluating the efficiency of proposed outlays." The Committee on Estimates has 30 members all from Lok Sabha (not both Houses), making Option A incorrect. Neither committee can summon Ministers (Option C is incorrect for both). Both committees' reports are recommendatory, not legally binding (Option D is incorrect). The key functional difference is temporal: Estimates Committee evaluates proposed expenditure (ex-ante), while PAC audits past expenditure (post-ante) with CAG assistance.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Which of the following correctly describes the domestic legal effect of an executive agreement concluded by the President on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers?

options.t: It automatically becomes part of domestic law without any legislative action.
It is binding under international law but has no direct domestic effect unless implemented by a statute.
It requires ratification by Parliament under Article 253 before it can bind the Union.
It can amend the Constitution without a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson states that the executive may conclude executive agreements which are binding under international law but have no direct domestic effect unless implemented by statute. This distinguishes them from treaties that require domestic legislation under Article 253. Option A is incorrect because domestic effect requires legislation. Option C describes the treaty route, not executive agreements. Option D is contradicted by the Keshav Singh case, which held the President cannot ratify a treaty amending the Constitution without an Article 368 amendment.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Regarding the appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), which statement is accurate in light of recent procedural developments?

options.t: The Prime Minister can unilaterally appoint the CAG without any consultative mechanism.
The President appoints the CAG on the advice of the Council of Ministers, but recent rules mandate a selection committee.
The CAG is appointed by a collegium of judges similar to the higher judiciary.
The appointment of the CAG requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson notes that while the formal appointing authority is the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers (headed by the Prime Minister), recent rules mandate a selection committee for key constitutional posts such as the CAG and CEC. Option A reflects the outdated assumption the lesson warns against. Option C confuses the CAG with judicial appointments governed by the collegium. Option D is incorrect because no constitutional amendment is needed for the CAG's appointment.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: The Cabinet Secretariat is best characterised as:

options.t: A political office akin to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).
A permanent civil‑service body governed by the Transaction of Business Rules.
A constitutional authority established under Article 77 of the Constitution.
An ad‑hoc body constituted only during national emergencies.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson explicitly states that the Cabinet Secretariat is a permanent civil‑service body governed by the Transaction of Business Rules, and warns against treating it as a political office akin to the PMO. It is not a constitutional authority under Article 77 (which deals with conduct of business), nor is it an ad‑hoc emergency body. Its role includes crisis management and inter‑ministerial coordination as a standing administrative structure.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: On what grounds can the Supreme Court strike down an ordinance promulgated by the President?

options.t: Only if the ordinance is not ratified by Parliament within the six‑week window.
If the ordinance is promulgated without the subjective satisfaction of the President.
For mala fides, re‑promulgation, or lack of urgency.
Only if the ordinance violates the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson outlines the evolving judicial standards: the Supreme Court can strike down ordinances for mala fides, re‑promulgation, or lack of urgency, as seen in the D.C. Wadhwa and Krishna Kumar Singh cases. While non‑ratification leads to lapse, it is not a ground for judicial striking down. The Court does not examine the President's subjective satisfaction (which is non‑justiciable), and basic structure violation is a broader ground not limited to ordinances.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Which statement correctly reflects the legal status of the Attorney General's advice to the Government of India?

options.t: The Attorney General's advice is binding on the executive and cannot be disregarded.
The Attorney General's advice is advisory; the government may reject it but must record reasons.
The Attorney General's opinion on judicial appointments overrides the collegium's recommendation.
The Attorney General is a member of the Cabinet and enjoys parliamentary privilege.

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson cites the 1998 State of Punjab v. Union of India case, which clarified that the AG's advice is not binding; the executive may reject it but must record reasons. Option A contradicts this principle. Option C is incorrect because the Third Judges case held the AG's opinion carries weight but does not override the collegium. Option D is false as the AG is not a Cabinet member and does not enjoy parliamentary privilege, though they may attend Cabinet meetings on legal issues.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: Under Article 85(1) of the Constitution, the President is obliged to summon each House of Parliament such that the maximum interval between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next session shall not exceed:
mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: Article 85(1) explicitly mandates that six months shall not intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next session. This constitutional ceiling ensures legislative accountability and prevents the executive from indefinitely avoiding parliamentary scrutiny. The 2020 winter session gap of 176 days (approximately 5.8 months) was criticized but did not breach this six-month limit, hence no judicial intervention occurred. The President acts on ministerial advice for summoning, but may return the recommendation if the gap threatens to exceed this constitutional limit.

mains-gs2/union-executive.text: In the National Security Council (NSC) constituted in 1998, who serves as the Secretary of the Council?

options.t: The Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister

mains-gs2/union-executive.sol: The lesson text states that the NSC is chaired by the Prime Minister and comprises key ministers, with the National Security Advisor (NSA) serving as its secretary. The NSA is the primary advisor to the Prime Minister on national security matters and coordinates the NSC's functioning. The Cabinet Secretary, while crucial for inter-ministerial coordination, is not the NSC Secretary. The NSC is an advisory body; the Prime Minister takes final decisions based on its recommendations.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.text: Under Article 112 of the Constitution, the Annual Financial Statement must distinguish between three specific funds. Which of the following correctly identifies these three funds and the key restriction on the Consolidated Fund?

options.t: Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, Public Account; no money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund without parliamentary authorisation
Consolidated Fund, Emergency Fund, Public Account; withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund require only executive approval
Revenue Fund, Capital Fund, Contingency Fund; the Consolidated Fund can be accessed through ordinances
Consolidated Fund, Development Fund, Public Account; parliamentary authorisation is required only for capital expenditure

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.sol: The lesson states that Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement to separate the Consolidated Fund, the Contingency Fund and the Public Account. It explicitly mentions that the Consolidated Fund receives all revenues, loans and recoveries, and 'no money can be withdrawn without parliamentary authorisation'. Option A correctly identifies all three funds and the key restriction. Option B incorrectly names 'Emergency Fund' and misstates the withdrawal rule. Option C uses incorrect fund names. Option D incorrectly names 'Development Fund' and limits parliamentary authorisation to capital expenditure only.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.text: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 originally targeted the elimination of the revenue deficit by 2008-09. What does a persistent revenue deficit indicate about the quality of public finances, according to the lesson?

options.t: It indicates that the government is borrowing to finance consumption, eroding the quality of public finances and limiting space for productive capital outlays
It indicates that capital expenditure is exceeding revenue receipts, requiring higher market borrowings for asset creation
It indicates that tax buoyancy has improved but non-tax revenues have declined, creating a temporary mismatch
It indicates that the primary deficit is being managed effectively while the fiscal deficit remains within FRBM targets

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.sol: The lesson explicitly states: 'A persistent revenue deficit signals that the state is borrowing to finance consumption, which erodes the quality of public finances and limits the space for productive capital outlays.' This matches option A exactly. Option B confuses revenue deficit with capital expenditure financing. Option C introduces tax buoyancy and non-tax revenues which are not mentioned in the revenue deficit explanation. Option D discusses primary deficit and fiscal deficit management, which are separate concepts from the revenue deficit's significance.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.text: During the GST compensation shortfall in 2020-21, the Centre borrowed funds and passed them to States as back-to-back loans. What was the primary fiscal rationale for this mechanism?

options.t: To preserve States' fiscal space without violating FRBM borrowing limits, while honouring the compensation guarantee
To increase the Centre's fiscal deficit temporarily while reducing States' debt-to-GDP ratios permanently
To shift the compensation burden to the RBI through monetised deficit financing
To allow States to exceed their FRBM borrowing limits with Centre's guarantee

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.sol: The lesson states: 'the centre eventually borrowed and passed on the funds as back-to-back loans, preserving the states' fiscal space without violating the FRBM borrowing limits.' This directly matches option A. Option B is incorrect because the mechanism was about preserving States' fiscal space, not reducing their debt-to-GDP ratios permanently. Option C mentions RBI monetised deficit financing, which is not mentioned in the lesson. Option D is incorrect because the whole point was to avoid violating FRBM borrowing limits, not to allow States to exceed them.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.text: According to the lesson, what is the key condition that allows a higher primary deficit without destabilising the debt-to-GDP ratio?

options.t: A favourable growth-interest differential where nominal GDP growth exceeds the effective interest rate on debt
A declining revenue deficit coupled with increasing capital expenditure financed by disinvestment proceeds
A reduction in the share of short-term treasury bills in the total debt portfolio
An increase in tax buoyancy through base broadening while maintaining subsidy levels

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.sol: The lesson explicitly states: 'Debt sustainability hinges on the differential between the nominal GDP growth rate and the effective interest rate on debt... A favourable growth-interest differential allows a higher primary deficit without destabilising the debt ratio.' This matches option A exactly. Option B mentions revenue deficit and disinvestment, which are policy levers but not the key condition for primary deficit sustainability. Option C discusses treasury bill share, which relates to rollover risk, not the growth-interest differential. Option D mentions tax buoyancy and subsidies as policy levers, not the fundamental condition.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.text: The lesson describes the classification of expenditure until 2017-18 and the subsequent change. Which statement accurately reflects this transition?

options.t: Expenditure was classified into plan and non-plan heads until 2017-18, when it was replaced by scheme-based classification
Expenditure was classified into revenue and capital heads until 2017-18, when plan/non-plan classification was introduced
Expenditure was classified into scheme-based heads until 2017-18, when it was replaced by plan/non-plan classification
Expenditure classification has remained unchanged since the FRBM Act, 2003, with only minor modifications in 2017-18

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.sol: The lesson states: 'Expenditure is classified into revenue and capital categories, and further into plan and non-plan heads until the planning nomenclature was replaced by the scheme-based classification in 2017-18.' Option A correctly captures this transition from plan/non-plan to scheme-based classification in 2017-18. Option B reverses the timeline and misstates the classifications. Option C also reverses the transition. Option D is incorrect because the lesson explicitly mentions a significant change in 2017-18, not minor modifications.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.text: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between the Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement (MTFPS) and the Fiscal Strategy Statement (FSS) under the FRBM Act?

options.t: MTFPS sets annual policy actions while FSS provides a rolling three‑year fiscal framework.
MTFPS is a statutory rolling three‑year target document; FSS translates those targets into concrete annual policy actions such as expenditure prioritisation and borrowing plans.
Both MTFPS and FSS are identical documents presented together in the Budget.
FSS is a standalone document not linked to the Union Budget.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.sol: The lesson states that the MTFPS is mandated under Section 4 of the FRBM Act and specifies three‑year targets for fiscal deficit, revenue deficit and debt‑to‑GDP. The FSS, distinct from the MTFPS, converts those medium‑term targets into annual policy measures — expenditure prioritisation, revenue measures and borrowing plans — for the forthcoming financial year. Therefore option B accurately captures this statutory‑operational linkage.

mains-gs3/fiscal-policy.text: According to the lesson, tax buoyancy is defined as the responsiveness of tax revenue to changes in nominal GDP holding tax policy constant. Which formula represents this definition?

options.t: (ΔTax Revenue / Tax Revenue) ÷ (ΔNominal GDP / Nominal GDP)
(ΔTax Revenue / Tax Revenue) ÷ (ΔReal GDP / Real GDP)
(ΔTax Revenue / Tax Revenue) ÷ (ΔTax Rate / Tax Rate)
(ΔTax Revenue / Tax Revenue) ÷ (ΔTax Base / Tax Base)
